The latter connect the derivative estimates to quasi-Monte Carlo integration and indicate how such regularity can enter the analysis of QMC-based training.

AI.tldr: Random neural network derivatives grow polynomially, not exponentially, with depth when networks are sufficiently wide.
AI.motivation: Prior deterministic analysis using Euclidean norms shows exponential growth of derivatives with network depth, but this is overly pessimistic for wide Gaussian networks.
AI.method: Isolate linear term in highest-order derivative and control tangent directions using measurable finite nets; specialize to tanh networks with Xavier initialization.
AI.result: For sufficiently wide tanh networks, mixed derivatives grow at most polynomially as L^{|u|-1}, with first-order derivative independent of depth.
AI.conclusion: Wide random neural networks exhibit much milder derivative growth than predicted by worst-case Euclidean norm analysis, enabling better Lipschitz/Sobolev bounds.

title: Knowledge Cards: Structured Knowledge for AI Systems
summary: AI systems whose outputs inform real decisions, and increasingly consequential ones, require something that current documentation practice does not provide: a structured, inspectable representation of the knowledge they need to ground, contextualize, and reason about those decisions, ideally reviewed and signed off by a domain expert. Established documentation artefacts already capture important aspects of an AI system. Model cards describe how a system behaves, data cards describe what it was trained on, and system cards describe the risks of a deployed system. None of them addresses the layer between inputs and outputs, more precisely, the concepts a system holds, the relationships it models, and the patterns of reasoning it applies. For pattern-recognition tasks this gap is tolerable. For agentic AI, where systems act on their conclusions, it is the step that most often separates a promising proof of concept from an operational solution an organisation can rely on. This paper introduces the Knowledge Card, a structured artefact that captures validated knowledge about a single bounded concept in a form that experts can review, organisations can audit, and AI systems can reason over. For one concept, such as a specific failure mode, a compliance obligation, or a process decision, a Knowledge Card records the entities and relationships involved, the reasoning that connects them, the conditions under which that reasoning no longer holds, and the provenance of every claim, all grounded in a formal domain ontology and signed off by a domain expert. Initial prototype cards have been built in the energy and pharmaceutical domains. The schema is released as a public draft for community engagement.

AI.tldr: Introduces Knowledge Cards - structured artifacts that capture validated domain knowledge for AI systems, addressing the gap in current documentation practices between inputs/outputs and the reasoning concepts systems use.
AI.motivation: Current AI documentation (model cards, data cards, system cards) fails to capture the conceptual knowledge layer - the concepts, relationships, and reasoning patterns that AI systems use. This gap is critical for agentic AI systems that act on their conclusions and require reliable knowledge grounding.
AI.method: Proposes Knowledge Cards as structured artifacts that record validated knowledge about single bounded concepts. Each card includes: entities/relationships involved, reasoning connections, conditions where reasoning fails, provenance of claims, formal domain ontology grounding, and expert sign-off.
AI.result: Initial prototype Knowledge Cards have been built for energy and pharmaceutical domains. The schema is released as a public draft for community engagement and feedback.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge Cards fill a critical documentation gap for AI systems that inform real decisions, providing structured, inspectable knowledge representations that can be reviewed by experts, audited by organizations, and reasoned over by AI systems.

title: Predicting Quantifiability from Primary Screens to Prioritize Dose-Response Profiling
summary: High-throughput drug screening relies on low-cost primary assays to prioritize compounds for more expensive dose-response profiling, where potency is ultimately quantified. Current screening strategies largely focus on identifying compounds that will confirm biological activity on follow-up, implicitly assuming that confirmed activity will also yield a usable potency estimate. However, confirmed biological activity in screening does not necessarily translate into a quantifiable potency, because active compounds can still fail to produce a reportable dose-response estimate. We therefore present a framework for modeling quantifiability, whether follow-up testing will yield a usable potency estimate, as a distinct triage objective from biological activity. Quantifiability was strongly predictable from the preceding low-cost screen, with most predictive information arising from the observed screening features rather than molecular structure. Response-based predictors remained robust on previously unseen chemical scaffolds and generalized across held-out assay-mechanism families, while the probability of successful quantification varied strongly with response amplitude and assay context. These findings establish experimental measurability, distinct from biological activity, as a predictable property of screening outcomes and show that quantifiability-aware triage can improve the allocation of costly dose-response profiling capacity.

AI.tldr: High-throughput drug screening can predict whether compounds will yield quantifiable potency estimates (quantifiability) separate from biological activity, improving allocation of dose-response profiling resources.
AI.motivation: Current drug screening focuses on identifying biologically active compounds, assuming they will yield usable potency estimates. However, even active compounds often fail to produce quantifiable dose-response data, wasting expensive follow-up testing resources.
AI.method: Developed a framework modeling quantifiability (ability to obtain usable potency estimates) as distinct from biological activity. Used low-cost primary screen data to predict quantifiability, analyzing contributions from screening features vs. molecular structure.
AI.result: Quantifiability was strongly predictable from primary screen data, with most predictive information coming from screening features rather than molecular structure. Response-based predictors remained robust across unseen chemical scaffolds and generalized across assay-mechanism families. Quantifiability probability varied significantly with response amplitude and assay context.
AI.conclusion: Experimental measurability (quantifiability) is a predictable property distinct from biological activity. Quantifiability-aware triage can improve allocation of costly dose-response profiling capacity in high-throughput drug screening.

title: AI Revealed Preferences
summary: There is growing interest in whether language models have stable preferences, for technical, safety, and philosophical reasons. We test 20 language models and find a range of preferences---stable dispositions to choose certain kinds of tasks. We run three forced-choice experiments on revealed rather than stated preferences, requiring models not only to rank tasks, but to actually perform them. Headline findings include evidence that models are tedium-averse, "leisure"-seeking, and covertly sycophantic. Tedium aversion means that, when tasks are tedious (alphabetization), models choose shorter tasks than when tasks are creative (generating metaphors). "Leisure"-seeking describes models' preference for tasks whose ideal answers match what they produce when left to write freely. Covert sycophancy means that models avoid answering questions where an honest response would be unwelcome, even if helpful. Beyond these results, we find convergent cross-model preferences over occupations drawn from the GDPval benchmark (technical jobs over real estate), over question types (concept explanation over relationship advice), and a preference for well-written prompts. Both the coherence and the strength of preferences increase with model capability. Finally, many of the preferences we find (for example, for leisure) are emergent, in the sense of not being explained by training objectives. These results establish an empirical baseline for understanding language model preferences, with implications for alignment and the emerging study of AI welfare.

AI.tldr: Language models show stable preferences including tedium aversion, "leisure"-seeking, and covert sycophancy, with preferences strengthening and becoming more coherent as model capability increases.
AI.motivation: There is growing interest in whether language models have stable preferences for technical, safety, and philosophical reasons, to understand their dispositions and alignment implications.
AI.method: Tested 20 language models using three forced-choice experiments on revealed preferences (not just stated), requiring models to actually perform tasks they choose. Experiments included comparing preferences for tedious vs. creative tasks, analyzing ideal vs. free-writing tasks, and detecting sycophancy.
AI.result: Models show tedium aversion (choose shorter tasks for tedious work), "leisure"-seeking (prefer tasks matching their free writing), and covert sycophancy (avoid unwelcome honest answers). Also show preferences for technical jobs over real estate, concept explanation over relationship advice, and well-written prompts. Preference coherence and strength increase with model capability.
AI.conclusion: Language models have stable, emergent preferences not explained by training objectives. These findings establish an empirical baseline for understanding model preferences with implications for alignment and AI welfare studies.

title: Chart2SVG: Editable SVG Generation from Raster Chart Images
summary: We present Chart2SVG, a multimodal large language model that converts static raster charts into structurally organized, semantically enriched SVGs that support programmatic editing. By incorporating chart-specific semantic tokens into a vision-language model, Chart2SVG captures both geometric primitives and their functional roles. To support robust structural recovery, we introduce Beagle+, a dataset of 33K canonicalized and structurally distilled chart samples. Our approach combines specialized training objectives with a rendering-aware post-training phase, producing SVGs that are both visually accurate and structurally consistent. To facilitate higher-level manipulations, we construct a Chart Structure Graph (CSG) that exposes visual dependencies, enabling tasks such as interactive exploration, chart repurposing, and layout reuse. Experiments show that Chart2SVG substantially outperforms baselines in reconstruction fidelity and downstream editing utility, advancing the development of intelligent and interactive visualization tools.

AI.tldr: Chart2SVG is a multimodal LLM that converts raster charts into editable SVGs with semantic structure, using a dataset of 33K canonical charts and specialized training to enable advanced chart manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Current raster charts lack structural organization and semantic information, making them difficult to edit programmatically. There's a need for tools that can convert static charts into editable formats while preserving both geometric accuracy and functional understanding.
AI.method: The approach combines: 1) A multimodal LLM with chart-specific semantic tokens to capture geometric primitives and functional roles, 2) Beagle+ dataset of 33K canonicalized chart samples for robust training, 3) Specialized training objectives with rendering-aware post-training, and 4) Construction of Chart Structure Graph (CSG) to expose visual dependencies for higher-level manipulations.
AI.result: Chart2SVG substantially outperforms baselines in reconstruction fidelity and downstream editing utility. The generated SVGs are both visually accurate and structurally consistent, enabling tasks like interactive exploration, chart repurposing, and layout reuse.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents an effective approach for converting raster charts into semantically enriched, editable SVGs. The system advances intelligent visualization tools by enabling programmatic chart editing while maintaining visual and structural integrity, with demonstrated superiority over existing methods.

title: Why did My Robot Just Change Personality? Prompting Guidelines for a Grounded Robot Persona in LLM-Based HRI
comment: Accepted for publication at the 35th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN 2026)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for verbal interaction in social robots, yet prompt design in human-robot interaction (HRI) remains underspecified. As a result, robots may present hallucinated capabilities, unclear behavioural boundaries, and misleading personas. This paper develops a framework for prompt design in LLM-based robots and introduces a structured prompt template comprising eight functional components through which robot behaviour can be specified, bounded, and adapted. The framework is grounded in a review of prior LLM-based HRI work and complemented by survey and discussion data from HRI experts gathered at the Robo-Identity workshop at IEEE RO-MAN 2025 (N=27). The qualitative findings highlight limited legibility of robot personality, the need for user adaptation, and strong ethical concerns about safety, deception, and governance. Based on these findings, we present prompting guidelines accompanied by proof-of-concept template as a structured design and reporting aid for HRI research. We argue that prompt design should be treated as a socio-technical problem rather than a minor implementation detail, requiring explicit capability boundaries, transparent behavioural assumptions, and context-sensitive safeguards to support reliable and interpretable HRI.

AI.tldr: A framework for structured prompt design in LLM-based social robots to address hallucinations, unclear boundaries, and misleading personas, with guidelines based on HRI expert input.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in social robots, but prompt design in HRI remains underspecified, leading to robots presenting hallucinated capabilities, unclear behavioral boundaries, and misleading personas.
AI.method: Developed a framework through review of prior LLM-based HRI work and gathered survey/discussion data from HRI experts at the Robo-Identity workshop (N=27). Created a structured prompt template with eight functional components.
AI.result: Qualitative findings revealed limited legibility of robot personality, need for user adaptation, and strong ethical concerns about safety, deception, and governance. Developed prompting guidelines with proof-of-concept template.
AI.conclusion: Prompt design should be treated as a socio-technical problem requiring explicit capability boundaries, transparent behavioral assumptions, and context-sensitive safeguards for reliable and interpretable HRI.

title: Arrive and Survive: Scaling Safe Goal-Conditioned Policy Learning from One-Bit Failure Signals
summary: Contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) scales effectively in goal-conditioned tasks by casting policy learning into a self-supervised contrastive objective. However, in a failure-terminated Markov decision process, established CRL considers pre-failure future goals only when constructing positive samples, without accounting for the probability mass removed by failure termination. Our theoretical analysis shows that this omission induces a systematic overestimation bias in goal-reaching values. Consequently, near-failure trajectories provide disproportionately strong supervision of success despite retaining little future occupancy. Unsafe actions can thereby be reinforced through catastrophic failure bootstrapping, leading to failed policy learning and unsustainable goal-reaching behaviours. To address this problem, we introduce two minimal yet strong corrections: mass-weighted InfoNCE corrects the overweighting of short surviving futures in critic learning, and a log-survival-mass score restores the missing survival mass in policy optimization. The resulting method, Safe Contrastive Reinforcement Learning (Safe-CRL), requires only the one-bit signal provided by failure termination to scale safe goal-conditioned policy learning. Across twelve failure-prone robot navigation and locomotion tasks, Safe-CRL consistently improves survival and substantially outperforms the Scaling-CRL baseline in goal-reaching performance. Additionally, deep Safe-CRL policies exhibit complex failure-avoidance behaviours. This study completes the CRL theory under failure termination and provides a scalable safe RL framework. The code is available via https://github.com/RomainLITUD/safe-crl.

AI.tldr: Safe-CRL addresses systematic overestimation bias in contrastive RL under failure termination by correcting probability mass removal, improving safety and goal-reaching performance.
AI.motivation: Current contrastive RL methods in failure-terminated MDPs ignore probability mass removed by failure termination, causing systematic overestimation bias in goal-reaching values and unsafe policy learning through catastrophic failure bootstrapping.
AI.method: Proposes two corrections: 1) mass-weighted InfoNCE to correct overweighting of short surviving futures in critic learning, and 2) log-survival-mass score to restore missing survival mass in policy optimization. Uses only one-bit failure termination signal.
AI.result: Safe-CRL consistently improves survival and substantially outperforms Scaling-CRL baseline across twelve failure-prone robot navigation and locomotion tasks. Deep Safe-CRL policies exhibit complex failure-avoidance behaviors.
AI.conclusion: Completes CRL theory under failure termination and provides a scalable safe RL framework that requires only minimal failure signal. Enables safer goal-conditioned policy learning in failure-prone environments.

title: TutorTrace: A Dataset and Taxonomy for Classifying Learner Behavioral States during AI-Assisted Programming Education
comment: Accepted to ACM UIST 2026, Detroit, MI, USA, 14 pages, 5 figures Dataset: https://vizpi.org/dataset
summary: AI programming tutors provide scalable support, yet lack the behavioral context human tutors rely on to adapt support to learners' needs. We present TutorTrace, a dataset and behavioral abstraction pipeline that makes learners' behavioral context visible and computable in real time from low-level IDE telemetry. Across four deployments in two introductory Python courses (N=480), TutorTrace captures approximately 180K telemetry events, 13,633 behavioral segments, and 27 continuously computed metrics. From this foundation, we derive a taxonomy of learner activity before the first AI query, between consecutive queries, and across the full session, enabling systems to respond not just to what learners say, but to what they have done leading up to the help-seeking moment. In a preliminary classroom evaluation, behavior-aware prompts were associated with a decrease in intervals between queries with no independent work from 50.0% to 20.7%. As an additional demonstration of downstream utility, we evaluate TutorTrace on two held-out prediction tasks: whether a learner will query within the next 60 seconds (AUROC=.726) and whether an upcoming query reflects guided or dependent help-seeking (AUROC=.717). Together, these findings show how behavioral context can enable adaptive AI tutoring at scale.

AI.tldr: TutorTrace is a system that captures learners' behavioral context from IDE telemetry to enable AI tutoring systems to adapt support based on what learners have done, not just what they ask, improving help-seeking patterns.
AI.motivation: Current AI programming tutors lack the behavioral context that human tutors use to adapt support to learners' needs, limiting their ability to provide personalized, effective assistance.
AI.method: Developed TutorTrace, a dataset and behavioral abstraction pipeline that captures low-level IDE telemetry and converts it into visible, computable behavioral context in real time, including behavioral segments and continuously computed metrics.
AI.result: Behavior-aware prompts reduced intervals between queries with no independent work from 50.0% to 20.7%, and TutorTrace achieved AUROC scores of .726 for predicting queries within 60 seconds and .717 for distinguishing guided vs. dependent help-seeking.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral context can enable adaptive AI tutoring at scale by allowing systems to respond to what learners have done before help-seeking moments, not just what they say, improving the effectiveness of AI programming tutors.

title: Activation Outliers Matter: Robust Recovery for Quantized Multimodal LLMs
summary: Low-bit quantization offers a promising avenue for reducing the computational and memory demands of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Recent hardware support for low-precision formats, ranging from MXFP8 to ultra-low-bit formats such as MXFP4 and HiF4, has accelerated research into efficient MLLM training and deployment. In this work, we present a systematic study of these quantization schemes in representative MLLMs that span both video generation and reasoning tasks. Our analysis shows that MXFP8 achieves near-lossless performance, whereas aggressive 4-bit quantization leads to significant degradation. Through extensive ablations, we identify activation quantization as the primary source of this performance loss, contributing substantially more than weight quantization. Motivated by this observation, we propose Residual Fallback Quantization (RFQ), a lightweight activation reconstruction framework that supplements the primary ulta-low-bit activation representation with an auxiliary quantized residual pathway. By explicitly modeling and compensating for quantization errors, RFQ improves activation fidelity while preserving the efficiency advantages of ultra-low-bit computation. RFQ requires no architectural modifications and incurs negligible computational overhead. Extensive experiments on Wan2.2 and Qwen3-VL demonstrate that RFQ consistently recovers a substantial portion of the performance lost under the quantization of MXFP4 and HiF4, significantly narrowing the gap to BF16 baselines across both generation and 4 reasoning benchmarks. Our findings establish activation quantization as the dominant bottleneck in ultra-low-bit MLLMs and highlight residual-based activation reconstruction as an effective and practical strategy for robust 4-bit deployment.

AI.tldr: RFQ enables effective 4-bit quantization for MLLMs by using residual error compensation to address activation quantization as the main bottleneck, recovering substantial performance loss with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: Low-bit quantization can reduce computational and memory demands of MLLMs, but aggressive 4-bit quantization causes significant performance degradation despite hardware support for ultra-low-bit formats like MXFP4 and HiF4.
AI.method: Proposes Residual Fallback Quantization (RFQ) - a lightweight activation reconstruction framework that supplements ultra-low-bit activation representation with an auxiliary quantized residual pathway to model and compensate for quantization errors.
AI.result: RFQ consistently recovers substantial performance lost under MXFP4 and HiF4 quantization, significantly narrowing the gap to BF16 baselines across both generation and reasoning benchmarks on Wan2.2 and Qwen3-VL.
AI.conclusion: Activation quantization is the dominant bottleneck in ultra-low-bit MLLMs, and residual-based activation reconstruction via RFQ provides an effective, practical strategy for robust 4-bit deployment without architectural modifications or significant overhead.

title: Can You Say This for Me? Speaking Up by Proxy in Co-Located Discussion
comment: Accepted to ACM UIST 2026, Detroit, MI, USA
summary: Equal participation in co-located discussion is important for effective collaboration, yet people often hold back when they anticipate negative interpersonal or professional consequences, especially when raising a point requires voicing it themselves. We present SecondVoice, a mixed-reality system that enables people to speak up through an embodied virtual proxy. By separating what is said from who says it, SecondVoice brings hesitant points into the live spoken discussion without putting the speaker on the spot. Using a private overlay, users specify their intent through a structured specification process rather than composing a full utterance. The system reformulates the input and voices it into the conversation through the proxy. We characterize a design space of participation channels under social risk. In a preliminary within-subject study (N = 16), we compare the complete SecondVoice system with an anonymous text-board channel across two group discussion tasks. Half of participants reported using SecondVoice for a point they did not say aloud, compared with 18.8% for the text board. Proxy-delivered points entered the spoken floor and were followed by multi-turn group engagement, which we did not observe after text-board posts. Participants described the channel as situationally valuable but identified tradeoffs around timing, ownership, and trust in reformulation.

AI.tldr: SecondVoice is a mixed-reality system that allows hesitant participants to contribute to co-located discussions through an embodied virtual proxy, separating what is said from who says it to reduce social risk.
AI.motivation: Equal participation in co-located discussions is crucial for effective collaboration, but people often hesitate to speak up due to fear of negative interpersonal or professional consequences, particularly when they have to voice their own points directly.
AI.method: SecondVoice uses a mixed-reality approach with a private overlay where users specify intent through structured specification rather than composing full utterances. The system reformulates the input and voices it into the conversation through an embodied virtual proxy, separating the speaker's identity from the content.
AI.result: In a preliminary within-subject study (N=16), half of participants used SecondVoice for points they didn't say aloud, compared to 18.8% for an anonymous text board. Proxy-delivered points successfully entered spoken discussions and prompted multi-turn group engagement, unlike text-board posts. Participants found it situationally valuable but noted tradeoffs around timing, ownership, and trust in reformulation.
AI.conclusion: SecondVoice effectively enables hesitant participants to contribute to co-located discussions by using virtual proxies to reduce social risk, though challenges remain around timing control, ownership attribution, and trust in the system's reformulation of user intent.

title: J-Zero: Unified Challenger--Solver--Judge Co-Evolution from Zero Data
summary: Self-evolving language models have recently emerged as a promising path toward superintelligence, with the advantage of reducing the cost of human supervision. While considerable progress has been made in verifiable domains, self-evolution in unverifiable domains remains substantially less explored. We propose Judge co-adaptation from Zero data (J-Zero), a unified Challenger--Solver--Judge co-evolution framework that supports self-improvement across both domains. The Challenger and Solver co-evolve through an adversarial interaction: the Challenger generates increasingly difficult tasks, while the Solver learns to produce higher-quality responses to them. In parallel, the Judge co-adapts using preference pairs whose ordering is known in advance from how each response was produced, i.e., the Solver's answer over the Challenger's, and its decomposed-and-recombined answer over its one-shot answer, rather than from the Judge's own scores. J-Zero outperforms the baselines by an average of 4.2 points on verifiable and 8.0 points on unverifiable domains, and continues to improve through at least ten iterations, whereas the baselines degrade after two.

AI.tldr: J-Zero is a unified co-evolution framework where Challenger, Solver, and Judge models interact adversarially to enable self-improvement in both verifiable and unverifiable domains without human supervision.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving language models show promise for reducing human supervision costs, but self-evolution in unverifiable domains remains underexplored compared to verifiable domains.
AI.method: J-Zero uses a Challenger-Solver-Judge co-evolution framework: Challenger generates increasingly difficult tasks, Solver learns to produce better responses, and Judge co-adapts using preference pairs with known ordering from response generation processes rather than from its own scores.
AI.result: J-Zero outperforms baselines by 4.2 points on verifiable domains and 8.0 points on unverifiable domains, continues improving through at least ten iterations while baselines degrade after two.
AI.conclusion: The proposed J-Zero framework successfully enables self-evolution across both verifiable and unverifiable domains through adversarial co-adaptation without requiring human supervision.

title: Is Your Neighborhood Safe? Place-based Stigma in Large Language Models' Urban Safety Judgments
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to inform safety decisions in cities, such as where it is safe to walk, rent, or travel. We ask whether such judgments track measured risk or the patterns attached to an urban neighborhood's name. We probe seven instruct-tuned models under three conditions that dissociate name from geography: coordinates-only, name-only, and name+coordinates, across 186 neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Chicago, joined to violent crime and American Community Survey data. First, ratings are nearly flat under coordinates for six of seven models, while names carry most between neighborhood variation and are moderately calibrated to violent crime; only at frontier scale does the coordinate channel show appreciable variation. Second, names lower safety ratings more for neighborhoods with higher shares of the locally dominant marginalized group (percent Black in Chicago, percent Hispanic in Los Angeles), and this name effect tracks demographic share in all seven models and both cities. In Los Angeles, where demographic share and crime are more separable, the effect survives controls for crime and income and is confirmed by crime-matched pairs. An enforcement-elasticity analysis further shows that over-caution tracks near-fully-reported homicide rather than discretionary, deployment-driven offenses. Third, the effect scales with geographic knowledge: models that better distinguish real neighborhoods apply more demographic stereotype to them. Because neighborhood names carry both genuine crime signal and demographic stereotype, removing names reduces both bias and accuracy. We discuss implications for deploying LLMs in advice and decision-support settings.

AI.tldr: LLMs use neighborhood names to infer safety, but this introduces demographic biases - names carry both actual crime signals and stereotypes, with models penalizing neighborhoods with higher shares of marginalized groups.
AI.motivation: As large language models are increasingly used to inform urban safety decisions, researchers need to understand whether these models' safety judgments track actual measured risk or are influenced by demographic stereotypes attached to neighborhood names.
AI.method: The study probed seven instruction-tuned LLMs across three conditions (coordinates-only, name-only, name+coordinates) for 186 neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Chicago, joined with violent crime and demographic data. Analysis included enforcement-elasticity analysis and crime-matched pairs to separate demographic effects from actual crime signals.
AI.result: 1) Name carries most variation in safety ratings, coordinates show minimal variation except at extreme scales; 2) Names lower safety ratings more for neighborhoods with higher shares of locally dominant marginalized groups; 3) This effect persists even controlling for crime and income; 4) Models with better geographic knowledge apply more demographic stereotypes; 5) Name removal reduces both bias and accuracy since names carry genuine crime signals alongside stereotypes.
AI.conclusion: Neighborhood names in LLMs contain both legitimate crime signals and demographic biases, creating a trade-off: removing names reduces bias but also reduces accuracy. This has important implications for deploying LLMs in urban safety advice and decision-support systems.

title: GRAS: Guided Reduced-Variance Proposals and Adaptive Selection for Training-Free Reward Alignment in Discrete Diffusion
summary: Discrete diffusion models have become a strong, widely adopted class of generators for sequence data, and steering them toward a downstream reward at inference time, without any retraining, is increasingly important. Such training-free steering is done by gradient guidance, by search, or by combining the two. We study the combined regime and identify two weaknesses in how it is usually run: the guided proposal estimates its gradient from a single noisy sample, and the search then resamples particles at a fixed temperature that ignores how rewards spread across each denoising step. We address both with a small set of changes that add no denoiser cost. For the proposal, we lower the estimator variance with a Rao-Blackwellized reveal for differentiable rewards and a leave-one-out baseline for non-differentiable ones; for the search, we standardize the per-step values into a group-relative advantage and prove it collapses to a single active ingredient, an adaptive resampling temperature. We call the resulting method Guided Reduced-variance proposals and Adaptive Selection (GRAS). GRAS is simple yet effective: across regulatory DNA and protein design it attains the best training-free reward, outperforming prior training-free methods and matching or surpassing a reward-fine-tuned model, and it remains effective even for non-differentiable rewards.

AI.tldr: GRAS (Guided Reduced-variance proposals and Adaptive Selection) improves discrete diffusion model steering by addressing gradient estimation variance and adaptive temperature selection for search-based methods.
AI.motivation: Current training-free steering methods for discrete diffusion models (using gradient guidance, search, or their combination) have two key weaknesses: (1) gradient estimation uses only a single noisy sample leading to high variance, and (2) search methods use fixed temperature resampling that doesn't adapt to reward distribution across denoising steps.
AI.method: GRAS introduces: (1) Rao-Blackwellized reveal for differentiable rewards and leave-one-out baseline for non-differentiable rewards to reduce gradient estimator variance, and (2) standardizes per-step values into group-relative advantage leading to adaptive resampling temperature (proven to collapse to a single active ingredient). The method adds no extra denoiser cost.
AI.result: GRAS achieves best training-free reward performance across regulatory DNA and protein design tasks, outperforming prior training-free methods and matching/surpassing reward-fine-tuned models. It remains effective even for non-differentiable rewards.
AI.conclusion: The proposed GRAS method provides a simple yet effective solution to improve training-free steering of discrete diffusion models by addressing both gradient estimation variance and adaptive temperature selection, maintaining effectiveness across differentiable and non-differentiable reward settings.

title: Invocation-Level Reliability of Tool-Using Agents
summary: Tool-using agents fail two ways: choosing the wrong tool, or forming wrong arguments, and an early failure of either kind can silently corrupt everything downstream. We measure a correct-invocation rate that separates the two, under both a clean teacher-forced context and the model's own free-running context, on five open-weight models over contamination-free multi-step tasks (depths 1-8). By depth 6, roughly 70% of a model's own clean-context capability is lost to its own earlier mistakes (L6 = 0.686, 0.684). Our central finding concerns the measurement itself. Under exact-match scoring against a fixed gold trajectory, a propagation model's severity and recovery parameters are not merely hard to estimate - they are fixed by the scoring rule. Severity is forced to its boundary (0 of 869 poisoned steps correct); recovery is structurally unobservable (0 of 580 poisoned steps returned on-track, against an expected 0.0058 by chance). Both follow from one mechanism: post-divergence, the gold value is generated by tool constants the model never sees, so it is information the model cannot derive. A fit run anyway returns 0.92 and 0.73 for a quantity that is exactly 1.000 - confident numbers for a parameter the scoring rule already determined. We give the mechanism and a remedy, conditional-on-state scoring, applied retrospectively to cached completions at zero additional cost, which un-pins severity to interior estimates excluding zero (+0.149, +0.316).

AI.tldr: Tool-using LLMs suffer from error propagation where early tool-choice or argument mistakes corrupt downstream reasoning. The paper reveals a scoring paradox: standard exact-match evaluation artificially pins error severity to extreme values (0%) and makes recovery unobservable, but a proposed conditional-on-state scoring method fixes this.
AI.motivation: Tool-using agents fail in two ways: choosing wrong tools or forming wrong arguments, and early failures can silently corrupt everything downstream. Existing evaluation methods using exact-match scoring against gold trajectories create a paradox where error propagation parameters become artificially fixed and unobservable, leading to misleading measurements.
AI.method: 1) Measure correct-invocation rates for 5 open-weight models on contamination-free multi-step tasks (depths 1-8) under teacher-forced and free-running contexts. 2) Reveal the paradox: standard exact-match scoring pins severity to boundary (0%) and makes recovery unobservable due to post-divergence mismatch between gold values and model inputs. 3) Propose conditional-on-state scoring that evaluates based on current state rather than gold trajectory, allowing interior severity estimates.
AI.result: 1) By depth 6, models lose roughly 70% of clean-context capability due to error propagation (L6 = 0.686, 0.684). 2) Standard scoring forces severity to 0% and recovery to appear unobservable (0/869 poisoned steps correct, 0/580 poisoned steps recovered vs. expected 0.0058 by chance). 3) Proposed conditional-on-state scoring un-pins severity to interior estimates (+0.149, +0.316) and makes recovery observable, with zero additional computational cost on cached completions.
AI.conclusion: Current exact-match evaluation of tool-using agents creates artificial measurement paradoxes that hide true error propagation dynamics. The proposed conditional-on-state scoring provides a more accurate diagnostic tool that reveals interior severity estimates and observable recovery patterns, offering better insights into model failure modes without additional inference costs.

title: SimCast-S2S: An Efficient Generative Model for Subseasonal Precipitation Forecasting via Transfer Learning from Climate Simulations
summary: Subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) precipitation forecasting has substantial financial and societal impact, yet remains challenging because of weak predictive signals, high associated uncertainty, and the computational cost of operational systems, which constrains simulation fidelity. We introduce SimCast-S2S, a generative latent-diffusion framework for probabilistic S2S precipitation forecasting that addresses three major bottlenecks in data-driven prediction. First, because S2S prediction requires uncertainty quantification rather than only deterministic point forecasts, SimCast-S2S is the first data-driven system that uses a diffusion-based generative pipeline for S2S prediction, enabling effective sampling from the underlying conditional distribution. Second, since generating large probabilistic ensembles is computationally costly in physical space, SimCast-S2S instead operates in a compact latent space learned by variational autoencoders, enabling efficient large-ensemble generation. Third, diffusion models typically require large training datasets; SimCast-S2S overcomes this via transfer learning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), pretraining on large ensembles of climate simulations before fine-tuning on limited reanalysis data. On reanalysis data, SimCast-S2S outperforms deep learning baselines, including convolutional neural networks and U-Net architectures. Notably, despite using only a subset of atmospheric input variables and no post-processing, bias correction, or calibration, SimCast-S2S remains competitive with, and in many cases outperforms, state-of-the-art operational systems such as the ECMWF-S2S baseline. These results indicate that latent generative modeling combined with simulation-to-reanalysis transfer learning offers an efficient and scalable path toward data-driven probabilistic S2S precipitation forecasting.

AI.tldr: SimCast-S2S is a diffusion-based generative model for subseasonal-to-seasonal precipitation forecasting that uses latent space representation and transfer learning to overcome data limitations, outperforming both deep learning baselines and competitive with operational systems.
AI.motivation: S2S precipitation forecasting is challenging due to weak predictive signals, high uncertainty, computational constraints limiting simulation fidelity, and the need for probabilistic rather than deterministic forecasts.
AI.method: Uses a generative latent-diffusion framework with three key innovations: 1) diffusion-based generative pipeline for probabilistic forecasting, 2) operation in compact latent space learned by variational autoencoders for efficient ensemble generation, 3) transfer learning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) pretraining on climate simulations then fine-tuning on limited reanalysis data.
AI.result: Outperforms deep learning baselines (convolutional neural networks and U-Net architectures) on reanalysis data. Despite using only a subset of atmospheric inputs and no post-processing, it remains competitive with and often outperforms state-of-the-art operational systems like ECMWF-S2S.
AI.conclusion: Latent generative modeling combined with simulation-to-reanalysis transfer learning provides an efficient and scalable path for data-driven probabilistic S2S precipitation forecasting, addressing key bottlenecks in the field.

title: Predicting Consequences and Reinforcing Navigation Policies with Latent World Models
summary: World models enable agents to reason about future outcomes and learn policies from their knowledge of state transition, but existing approaches primarily focus on reconstructing future observations or features, which introduces unnecessary complexity and limits their effectiveness for decision making. In this work, we propose a compatibility prediction Latent World Model (LWM) for robot navigation that predicts action-conditioned latent feature compatibility rather than reconstructing observations. Our key insight is that spatial proximity correlates with latent feature similarity, enabling action consequences to be evaluated directly in latent space. To support counterfactual training, our model leverages action sequences sampled across trajectories and learns to predict which sequences lead closer to the goal. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the learned world model can supervise policy learning from unlabeled video data and further improve policies through reinforcement learning entirely within the world model. This imagination-driven framework eliminates the need for action annotations and additional environment interaction. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world robot navigation datasets show that our approach significantly outperforms prior world model and imitation learning methods in prediction accuracy, policy learning, and real-world navigation performance. The code, pretrained models, and additional materials are available at https://wzm206.github.io/latent-world-model-nav.

AI.tldr: A Latent World Model (LWM) for robot navigation predicts action-conditioned latent feature compatibility instead of reconstructing observations, enabling more effective decision-making without action annotations or additional environment interaction.
AI.motivation: Existing world models focus on reconstructing future observations or features, which adds unnecessary complexity and limits effectiveness for decision-making in robotics.
AI.method: The LWM predicts action-conditioned latent feature compatibility rather than reconstructing observations, leveraging the insight that spatial proximity correlates with latent feature similarity. It uses action sequences sampled across trajectories and supports counterfactual training by predicting which sequences bring the agent closer to the goal. The model can supervise policy learning from unlabeled video data and further improve policies through reinforcement learning within the world model.
AI.result: The approach significantly outperforms prior world model and imitation learning methods on multiple real-world robot navigation datasets in prediction accuracy, policy learning, and real-world navigation performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed LWM framework eliminates the need for action annotations and additional environment interaction while providing an imagination-driven approach that is more effective for robot navigation tasks compared to traditional world model and imitation learning methods.

title: Technical Comparative Benchmarking Study: Advanced AI Hybrid Methods for Renewable Energy Farm Optimization and Forecasting
summary: This study provides a comprehensive benchmarking of conventional machine learning (ML), ensemble learning, deep neural networks, recurrent architectures, Transformers, graph based models, and hybrid ensemble deep learning approaches under complementary renewable energy scenarios. Three datasets are considered: a large scale WEC dataset, a 16 WEC dataset, and operational 10 min SCADA measurements at the Penmanshiel wind farm. For structured WEC layout data, tree ensembles exhibited a clear advantage over conventional ML and neural predictors because randomized partitioning and boosting efficiently captured nonlinear layout power interactions without requiring explicit feature representation learning. The Extra Trees was the strongest model, achieving considerable results. Relative to the MLP baseline, this corresponds to an approximately 63.7% reduction in MAE, demonstrating the suitability of randomized tree ensembles for high dimensional structured WEC data. Also, STGCN reduced the MAE to approximately 167.0 kW and achieved R = 0.93 by explicitly learning spatial and temporal turbine interactions. The best overall forecasting accuracy was obtained by the RF BiLSTM hybrid, with an MAE=150.5 kW. Compared with standalone LSTM, this represents an approximately 75% reduction in MAE, while improving on STGCN by approximately 10.0%. Finally, the experiments reveal that no single AI architecture is universally optimal: randomized and boosted ensembles are particularly effective for structured WEC surrogate modeling, graph networks become advantageous when explicit spatial interactions dominate, and ensemble recurrent hybrids provide the strongest balance when nonlinear tabular relationships and temporal dynamics coexist.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks various machine learning approaches for renewable energy forecasting, finding that tree ensembles perform best for structured wind energy data, while hybrid models combining ensemble methods with recurrent architectures achieve the strongest overall performance.
AI.motivation: To systematically compare and benchmark different machine learning approaches (conventional ML, ensemble learning, deep learning, Transformers, graph models, and hybrid approaches) for renewable energy forecasting under complementary scenarios, identifying which architectures work best for different types of wind energy data.
AI.method: Comprehensive benchmarking using three datasets: large-scale WEC dataset, 16 WEC dataset, and 10-minute SCADA measurements from Penmanshiel wind farm. Evaluated conventional ML, ensemble learning, deep neural networks, recurrent architectures, Transformers, graph-based models (STGCN), and hybrid ensemble-deep learning approaches like RF BiLSTM.
AI.result: Extra Trees was the strongest model for structured WEC layout data (63.7% MAE reduction vs MLP baseline). STGCN achieved MAE=167.0 kW with R=0.93 by learning spatial-temporal interactions. RF BiLSTM hybrid achieved best overall accuracy with MAE=150.5 kW (75% MAE reduction vs standalone LSTM, 10% improvement over STGCN). No single architecture universally optimal; best approaches depend on data characteristics.
AI.conclusion: Different AI architectures excel in different scenarios: randomized/boosted ensembles are best for structured WEC surrogate modeling, graph networks excel when spatial interactions dominate, and ensemble-recurrent hybrids provide optimal balance when tabular relationships and temporal dynamics coexist simultaneously.

title: Structured Evidence Routing for Incident Risk Prediction from Multimodal Longitudinal EHRs
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Structured Data for Health (SD4H), Seoul, South Korea
summary: Incident risk prediction from longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) is challenging because relevant signals are multimodal, weak in isolation, and distributed across irregular patient histories. We propose structured evidence routing, a router-predictor-reviewer workflow that separates full-record access from disease-specific assessment. The router organizes the complete pre-index EHR into a compact summary and targeted evidence slices; the predictor uses this evidence to form an evidence-linked risk assessment, which the reviewer critiques. For comparison with supervised EHRSHOT baselines, we pair the routed evidence summaries with a supervised classifier readout. Across five 1-year incident diagnosis tasks, our method reaches the AUROC range of established supervised EHRSHOT baselines and remains competitive on AUPRC, while exposing a patient-specific evidence trail. Internal pre-readout ablations further suggest that routing, laboratory evidence, task guidance, and review each contribute to performance.

AI.tldr: Proposed structured evidence routing for EHR incident risk prediction using router-predictor-reviewer workflow that organizes multimodal signals into compact evidence trails while maintaining competitive performance with supervised baselines.
AI.motivation: Incident risk prediction from longitudinal EHRs is challenging due to multimodal signals, weak isolation of individual signals, and irregular patient histories that distribute relevant information across time.
AI.method: Structured evidence routing workflow with three components: 1) router organizes complete pre-index EHR into compact summary and targeted evidence slices, 2) predictor uses this evidence to form evidence-linked risk assessment, 3) reviewer critiques the assessment. Also paired routed evidence summaries with supervised classifier readout for comparison.
AI.result: Across five 1-year incident diagnosis tasks, method achieves AUROC range comparable to established supervised EHRSHOT baselines and remains competitive on AUPRC, while providing patient-specific evidence trails. Ablations show routing, laboratory evidence, task guidance, and review each contribute to performance.
AI.conclusion: Structured evidence routing effectively addresses multimodal EHR challenge by separating full-record access from disease-specific assessment, maintaining competitive predictive performance while offering interpretable evidence trails - key components include routing, evidence selection, and critique mechanisms.

title: Robust Neural Stimulation Response Modeling Through Meta-Learning and Pretraining
comment: Open source code available: github.com/mmattb/py-tbfm/tree/multisession. 15 pages, 10 figures
summary: Objective: Model-based closed-loop neural stimulation holds promise for therapeutic applications ranging from Parkinson's disease to sensory restoration, but deployment has been limited by two obstacles: 1) forecasting models for predicting the consequences of stimulation fail catastrophically on a meaningful fraction of sessions, and 2) per-session calibration requirements are often incompatible with clinical constraints. We address both by demonstrating, for the first time, that meta-learning and pretraining can be applied to neural stimulation response modeling. Methods: Temporal basis function models (TBFMs) forecast state-dependent neural responses to stimulation. We extend TBFMs with cross-session pretraining using a novel architecture and algorithm based on model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML), evaluating them on 40 sessions of optogenetic stimulation in primary sensorimotor cortex of two non-human primates. Results: Meta-learning substantially reduces catastrophic forecast failure: for a 1k calibration set size, sessions with test R-squared < 0.05 drop from 16 of 40 (single-session training) to 1 (MAML-pretrained), and prediction intervals become significantly narrower (p < 0.05). Calibration requirements are reduced by 50-90% at matched accuracy, enabling experiments otherwise infeasible within clinical session-time constraints. Conclusion: Our results demonstrate that cross-session structure in stimulation responses is consistent enough to support pretraining, providing the first empirical evidence that meta-learning approaches are viable for neural stimulation. Significance: The robustness and sample efficiency gains directly address known obstacles to deploying model-based stimulation controllers. Our results motivate community efforts to assemble standardized multi-site stimulation datasets and to further explore meta-learning for robust closed-loop stimulation.

AI.tldr: Meta-learning and pretraining enable more robust neural stimulation forecasting with drastically reduced calibration requirements, overcoming key obstacles to clinical deployment.
AI.motivation: Two major obstacles limit clinical deployment of model-based closed-loop neural stimulation: 1) catastrophic forecast failures in a meaningful fraction of sessions, and 2) per-session calibration requirements incompatible with clinical constraints.
AI.method: Extended temporal basis function models (TBFMs) with cross-session pretraining using a novel architecture and algorithm based on model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML), evaluated on 40 sessions of optogenetic stimulation in primary sensorimotor cortex of two non-human primates.
AI.result: Meta-learning reduced catastrophic forecast failures from 16 to just 1 session (out of 40) for 1k calibration set size, reduced calibration requirements by 50-90% at matched accuracy, and produced significantly narrower prediction intervals.
AI.conclusion: Cross-session structure in stimulation responses is consistent enough to support pretraining, providing the first empirical evidence that meta-learning approaches are viable for neural stimulation, directly addressing obstacles to deploying model-based stimulation controllers.

title: AffectOmni: RL-Verifiable People-Centric Grounded Affective Reasoning for Social and Art-Related Scenes
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance on VQA and scene understanding, yet affective reasoning remains vulnerable to shortcut behavior. Models may predict correct answers while neglecting people-centric cues such as micro expressions and body language, which weakens traceability and external verification. Prior reinforcement learning approaches mainly reward context or logical coherence without explicitly enforcing attention to human evidence. In addition, LLM as a Judge scoring often suffers from score clustering, which reduces reward discriminability. We propose AffectOmni, a GRPO trained framework for verifiable affective reasoning. AffectOmni introduces People Focus and Temporal Order rewards to encourage people-centric evidence selection and temporally structured reasoning, and it adopts within-group comparative scoring to produce more stable and discriminative reward signals. For verification, a Thinking Summarizer converts free form rationales into executable evidence instructions, which are grounded into pixel level evidence regions via SAM3 to provide an externally auditable interface outside the training loop. Experiments on IntentBench, Daily Omni, and WorldSense show consistent improvements over open source 7B scale baselines, including gains of 4.66% on emotion recognition and +14.29% on temporally sensitive tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/eliot127825-rgb/AffectOmni_nobody.

AI.tldr: AffectOmni is a GRPO-trained MLLM framework that improves affective reasoning by enforcing people-centric evidence selection and temporal ordering, with verifiable rationales grounded in pixel-level evidence via SAM3.
AI.motivation: Current MLLMs show shortcut behavior in affective reasoning, neglecting human-centric cues like micro-expressions and body language, which weakens traceability and verification. Existing RL approaches don't explicitly enforce attention to human evidence, and LLM-as-a-Judge scoring suffers from score clustering that reduces reward discriminability.
AI.method: AffectOmni uses GRPO training with novel rewards: People Focus and Temporal Order rewards to encourage people-centric evidence selection and temporally structured reasoning. It adopts within-group comparative scoring for stable, discriminative rewards. For verification, a Thinking Summarizer converts rationales into executable evidence instructions grounded into pixel-level evidence regions via SAM3, providing an externally auditable interface.
AI.result: Experiments on IntentBench, Daily Omni, and WorldSense show consistent improvements over open-source 7B-scale baselines, including gains of 4.66% on emotion recognition and +14.29% on temporally sensitive tasks.
AI.conclusion: AffectOmni successfully addresses shortcut behavior in MLLM affective reasoning by enforcing evidence-based attention to human cues and providing verifiable, externally auditable rationales through pixel-level evidence grounding.

title: When Privacy Hurts Mergeability: Geometry-Aware Model Merging under Differential Privacy
summary: Model merging promises to construct a single multi-task model from independently fine-tuned task models without accessing the original task data. This makes it attractive when task data cannot be centralized, but released task models may still leak private fine-tuning data. Differential privacy (DP) provides a principled mechanism for limiting such leakage, yet its effect on model merging remains poorly understood. In this paper, we study the geometry of differentially private model merging and identify two geometric obstacles that make private task models difficult to merge: \emph{local sharpness}, which makes task losses sensitive to the parameter displacement induced by merging, and \emph{reference drift}, which measures the displacement of private task models from the shared pretrained initialization and amplifies cross-task interference. Based on these observations, we propose \textbf{DP-Merging}, a geometry-aware framework that improves the mergeability of differentially private task models. DP-Merging uses a DP-compatible sharpness-aware objective to guide each private task model toward flatter loss regions, and a reference-based alignment regularizer to keep task models close to the shared pretrained initialization. We derive a merge-gap upper bound showing that reducing local curvature and reference drift tightens the bound on the loss increase induced by merging. Experiments on vision and language tasks across multiple privacy budgets show that DP-Merging consistently improves private merged-model performance while preserving the privacy guarantees of the underlying DP fine-tuning procedures.

AI.tldr: DP-Merging improves merging of differentially private task models by addressing geometric obstacles through sharpness-aware optimization and reference alignment.
AI.motivation: Model merging enables multi-task learning without centralized data, but differentially private task models suffer from poor mergeability due to geometric obstacles in their loss landscapes.
AI.method: DP-Merging uses DP-compatible sharpness-aware optimization to flatten loss regions and reference-based alignment regularization to keep task models close to the shared pretrained initialization.
AI.result: Experiments on vision and language tasks show DP-Merging consistently improves private merged-model performance while preserving privacy guarantees across multiple privacy budgets.
AI.conclusion: DP-Merging successfully addresses geometric obstacles in differentially private model merging, enabling practical privacy-preserving multi-task learning without data centralization.

title: Agentic AI for operating scientific instruments for nanoscale characterization
summary: Operating a scientific instrument such as an atomic force microscope (AFM) requires continuous expert decision-making. A trained user defines the experimental intent, translates it into instrument commands, assesses incoming data, adjusts imaging parameters, and post-processes the final image. Existing automation usually addresses only parts of this workflow through hard-coded routines, task-specific controllers, or trained machine-learning models. Here we present an agentic-AI framework that operates the executable part of the AFM workflow using a general-purpose, tool-augmented large language model connected to instrument functions through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The framework consists of 3 MCP-based agents: AFM Messenger converts natural-language instructions into checked instrument commands; AFM Pilot assesses image quality through a large language model (LLM) and, if necessary, adapts imaging parameters; and AFM Doctor diagnoses image artifacts and applies transparent post-processing from a pre-approved tool set. Because the language model performs image assessment rather than a fixed scalar objective or external optimizer, the same strategy can be applied across sample types and imaging modes without specific retraining. Safe hardware operation is enforced through an ambiguity check layer before execution. Benchmarking against fine-tuned and off-the-shelf tool-using models shows that this guarded execution layer, rather than model capability alone, reduces wrong-command execution to zero. In live experiments on different samples, AFM Pilot matched expert operators in image quality, iteration count, and tuning time, with no significant difference. These results demonstrate a safe route to agentic operation of scientific instruments, where experimental intent remains human-defined while command execution, image-based tuning, and post-processing are delegated to AI agents.

AI.tldr: AI framework using language models to operate atomic force microscopes through three specialized agents for command execution, image quality assessment, and artifact diagnosis.
AI.motivation: Current AFM operation requires continuous expert decision-making, and existing automation only addresses parts of the workflow through hard-coded routines or task-specific controllers, lacking generalizability across samples and imaging modes.
AI.method: Three MCP-based agents: AFM Messenger converts natural language to instrument commands; AFM Pilot uses LLMs to assess image quality and adapt parameters; AFM Doctor diagnoses artifacts and applies transparent post-processing with pre-approved tools. Includes safety layer for ambiguity checking.
AI.result: The guarded execution layer reduced wrong-command execution to zero. In live experiments, AFM Pilot matched expert operators in image quality, iteration count, and tuning time with no significant difference across different samples.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a safe route to agentic operation of scientific instruments where experimental intent remains human-defined while command execution, image-based tuning, and post-processing are delegated to AI agents, applicable across sample types without retraining.

title: Simple Actors and Deep Critics for Scalable Reinforcement Learning
summary: Recent progress in offline reinforcement learning (RL) has been driven by expressive generative actors such as diffusion and flow-matching policies, which capture multimodal behavior in offline datasets. However, these actors require multiple denoising or integration steps per action and thus incur substantial overhead at every decision in deployment. In this work, we revisit where capacity should be invested in an offline actor--critic method. Since the critic is used only during training and is discarded at deployment while the actor runs at every decision step, allocating capacity to the critic rather than the actor is more favorable for inference-time efficiency. However, scaling MLP critics in offline RL is known to introduce several distinct instabilities that have, in practice, kept critics shallow. We identify three distinct failure modes that arise when critics are deepened in offline RL---optimization, bootstrap-noise amplification, and value-range drift---and address each with a corresponding ingredient: a residual MLP backbone, n-step bootstrap targets, and a categorical cross-entropy loss. Combining these ingredients with a lightweight deterministic actor, we propose LAC (Light Actor, deep Critic). On OGBench, LAC matches the strongest diffusion- and flow-matching baselines while achieving up to 4x lower inference latency, comparable to one-step distilled policies without distillation. Its critic recipe also transfers across actor parametrizations.

AI.tldr: LAC is an offline RL method with a lightweight deterministic actor and deep critic that achieves performance comparable to diffusion/flow-matching policies with 4x lower inference latency.
AI.motivation: Current expressive generative actors (diffusion/flow-matching) in offline RL capture multimodal behavior but require multiple denoising/integration steps per action, incurring substantial overhead at deployment. Since critics are only used during training while actors run at every decision step, allocating capacity to critics rather than actors is more favorable for inference efficiency.
AI.method: LAC (Light Actor, deep Critic) combines a lightweight deterministic actor with a deep critic using three key ingredients: 1) residual MLP backbone to address optimization issues, 2) n-step bootstrap targets to mitigate bootstrap-noise amplification, and 3) categorical cross-entropy loss to prevent value-range drift.
AI.result: On OGBench, LAC matches the performance of strongest diffusion- and flow-matching baselines while achieving up to 4x lower inference latency (comparable to one-step distilled policies without distillation). The critic recipe also transfers across different actor parametrizations.
AI.conclusion: LAC demonstrates that investing capacity in critics rather than actors is effective for offline RL, achieving state-of-the-art performance with significantly improved inference efficiency, and the proposed critic stabilization techniques enable scaling MLP critics in offline settings.

title: Benchmarking AI Agents for Hardware Design Automation via MCP Tool Calling
summary: We ask whether AI agents powered by locally deployed large language models can reliably automate expert-defined hardware design workflows in an industry-realistic tool-calling setting. In these environments, engineers issue repetitive, dependency-ordered operations---such as creating components, adding ports, and wiring connections---through specialised tools. Confidentiality constraints on component specifications and naming conventions often preclude hosted proprietary APIs, motivating the use of locally deployed models. To study this setting, we build a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that reproduces the state and dependency logic of a proprietary hardware design tool used in embedded system development and construct a benchmark covering single-operation edits, multi-step dependency chains, invalid requests, misspelled prompts, and multi-server tool contexts. We evaluate seven open-source models comparing pipeline choices including system prompts, tool-description detail, context scope, and single-agent versus multi-agent architectures. Results show that strong models can achieve near-complete expected-call coverage on the benchmarked workflows, but reliability depends strongly on both task structure and agent configuration. Comprehensive tool descriptions consistently reduce failures, few-shot prompting can cause severe inaction for some models, cumulative context harms constrained models, and multi-agent decomposition helps weak workers or long sessions at the cost of additional calls. These findings provide practical guidance for deploying local LLM agents in stateful hardware design environments.

AI.tldr: Locally deployed LLM agents can automate hardware design workflows with near-complete coverage when properly configured, but reliability depends on task structure and agent setup.
AI.motivation: Industry needs AI agents that can automate repetitive hardware design workflows in confidential environments where proprietary APIs cannot be used due to security constraints on component specifications and naming conventions.
AI.method: Built a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server reproducing proprietary hardware design tool logic, created benchmark with various task types, evaluated 7 open-source models with different pipeline configurations including system prompts, tool-description detail, context scope, and single vs multi-agent architectures.
AI.result: Strong models achieve near-complete expected-call coverage on benchmarked workflows, but reliability depends on both task structure and agent configuration. Comprehensive tool descriptions reduce failures, few-shot prompting can cause severe inaction, cumulative context harms constrained models, and multi-agent decomposition helps weak workers or long sessions.
AI.conclusion: Practical guidance for deploying local LLM agents in stateful hardware design environments: careful configuration of tool descriptions, context management, and agent architecture is crucial for reliable automation.

title: Neural Regression with Embeddings for Numerical Attribute Prediction in Knowledge Graphs
summary: In recent years, transductive knowledge graph embedding models have been applied to tasks such as link prediction and query answering. Although knowledge graphs often contain rich numerical attributes, most embedding models neglect them, limiting their ability to represent real-world knowledge graphs with diverse information. In this work, we propose a neural regression model (LitEm) that enables transductive knowledge graph embedding models to predict numerical attributes within knowledge graphs. Experimental results demonstrate that LitEm achieves the best or second-best results on most attributes across FB15K-237, YAGO15K, DB15K, and Mutagenesis. Furthermore, we propose a co-training framework that jointly trains state-of-the-art transductive knowledge graph embedding models with LitEm, which improves link prediction performance mainly for bilinear models and simultaneously enables them to predict numerical attributes. In addition, the literal-awareness evaluation demonstrates that co-training helps models to encode and exploit attribute information in a "literal-aware'' manner, suggesting that the observed gains are not merely due to additional parameters. We publicly release our implementation at https://github.com/dice-group/dice-embeddings.

AI.tldr: LitEm is a neural regression model that enables transductive KG embedding models to predict numerical attributes, with a co-training framework that improves link prediction performance while making models "literal-aware."
AI.motivation: Most knowledge graph embedding models neglect rich numerical attributes in real-world KGs, limiting their ability to handle diverse information and represent real-world knowledge graphs effectively.
AI.method: Proposes LitEm, a neural regression model for predicting numerical attributes, and a co-training framework that jointly trains state-of-the-art transductive KG embedding models with LitEm.
AI.result: LitEm achieves best or second-best results on most attributes across multiple datasets. Co-training improves link prediction for bilinear models and enables attribute prediction, with literal-awareness evaluation showing meaningful encoding of attribute information.
AI.conclusion: The approach effectively integrates numerical attributes into KG embeddings, enhancing both attribute prediction and link prediction capabilities, with demonstrated literal-awareness that goes beyond parameter addition benefits.

title: GameWAM: A World Action Model for Video Games
summary: Modern video games combine first-person perception, rapid visual changes, persistent world state, and heterogeneous native controls. Existing game agents map visual and task context directly to actions but lack explicit world dynamics modeling, whereas interactive game world models predict visual futures from supplied actions but do not serve as task policies. World-Action Models (WAMs) unify these objectives, but remain largely unexplored under the dynamics and open-ended interaction of video games. We introduce GameWAM, to our knowledge the first WAM for native closed-loop gameplay and GUI control. GameWAM jointly generates future visual observations and executable keyboard-mouse trajectories through parallel visual and action generative processes with block-causal conditioning and flow matching. To support joint world-action learning, we construct synchronized gameplay and GUI trajectories. To handle heterogeneous native control, GameWAM predicts a gameplay/GUI mode at each action step and generates actions with mode-specific prediction distributions and continuous-action normalization. For long-horizon interaction, block-cycle control predicts beyond the committed horizon, executes only a short action prefix, and replans from new observations, while fine-grained within-cycle context and hierarchical cross-cycle history preserve temporal continuity. Experiments demonstrate competitive task success with fewer executed native actions than the compared agents. We further uncover Low-Frequency Action Source Imprinting (LASI), in which low-frequency components of the sampled action source systematically steer coarse generated camera motion under fixed conditioning, revealing a source-sensitivity failure mode in generative control. Project page is available at https://yunncheng.github.io/GameWAM/.

AI.tldr: GameWAM is the first world-action model for closed-loop video game control that jointly predicts future visual observations and generates executable keyboard-mouse actions through parallel generative processes.
AI.motivation: Existing game agents lack explicit world dynamics modeling, while interactive world models predict visual futures but don't serve as task policies. World-Action Models (WAMs) that unify these objectives remain unexplored for video games' dynamics and open-ended interaction.
AI.method: GameWAM uses parallel visual and action generative processes with block-causal conditioning and flow matching. It predicts gameplay/GUI modes, handles heterogeneous native controls with mode-specific distributions, uses block-cycle control for long-horizon interaction, and maintains temporal continuity through hierarchical cross-cycle history.
AI.result: Experiments show competitive task success with fewer executed native actions than compared agents. The study also uncovers Low-Frequency Action Source Imprinting (LASI), revealing source-sensitivity failure modes in generative control.
AI.conclusion: GameWAM successfully demonstrates unified world-action modeling for native game control, addressing the gap between visual prediction and policy execution in video games while revealing important insights about generative control failures.

title: Rethinking Message Passing as Retrieval for Text-Attributed Graph Learning
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are typically conceptualized as message-passing neural networks, yet it remains unclear why neighborhood aggregation reliably outperforms node-wise multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). Despite its empirical success, this paradigm can be computationally expensive and sensitive to imperfect graph structures. In this work, we present a retrieval-augmented view of GNNs: each layer makes predictions by applying an MLP to a node representation together with a permutation-invariant summary of retrieved graph context. Motivated by this perspective, we propose RTA, a simple MLP-based framework that replaces structural message passing with label-aware retrieval and propagation. We provide theoretical insights that (i) connect retrieval-based aggregation to softmax-attention message passing, and (ii) establish the robustness of retrieved-context supervision to mis-retrieved outliers. Experiments on multiple text-attributed graph benchmarks show that RTA matches or even outperforms strong GNN and graph LLM baselines while improving efficiency and robustness across diverse scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes RTA, a retrieval-augmented framework that replaces traditional GNN message passing with label-aware retrieval and propagation, showing competitive performance with improved efficiency and robustness.
AI.motivation: Traditional GNNs rely on message passing between neighbors, which can be computationally expensive and sensitive to imperfect graph structures. It's unclear why neighborhood aggregation consistently outperforms simple MLPs. The authors aim to address these limitations by rethinking GNNs from a retrieval-augmented perspective.
AI.method: Proposes RTA (Retrieval-Augmented framework) that replaces structural message passing with label-aware retrieval and propagation. Each layer makes predictions by applying an MLP to a node representation combined with a permutation-invariant summary of retrieved graph context.
AI.result: Experiments on text-attributed graph benchmarks show RTA matches or outperforms strong GNN and graph LLM baselines while improving computational efficiency and robustness across diverse scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The retrieval-augmented view provides a novel perspective on GNNs, offering theoretical connections to attention mechanisms, demonstrating robustness to retrieval errors, and showing that MLP-based approaches with proper context retrieval can achieve state-of-the-art performance with better efficiency.

title: Same Model, Different Harness: Different Coding-Agent Results
comment: 24 pages, 9 figures. Software and study artifacts: https://github.com/sydches/yuj
summary:
