A coding agent combines a model with a harness, which decides what the model sees, which tools it can use, and how the work continues. We ask whether changing the harness changes the result when the model and task stay fixed. We compare two configurations of the same harness on three coding benchmarks. The control supplies the full conversation in time order, while the treatment keeps the same record but mechanically shortens older tool results as the context fills and responds to repeated or stalled work.
  Under tight context, the treatment raises mean per-task fail-to-pass fraction (F2PF) in all three pressure comparisons and increases complete solutions on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro. The tight-window Verified comparison uses 169 tasks, a 20,480-token window, and a fixed 480-second attempt endpoint; on this cohort, treatment raises mean per-task F2PF from 28 percent to 49 percent and complete solutions from 43 to 72. Without model-specific retuning, the same frozen treatment also raises both endpoints on the same cohort for three additional models with different designs. In the wide-window Qwen3.6 comparisons, observed arm outcomes are close on Verified and Pro, while FeatureBench retains a higher mean per-task F2PF under treatment. On the wide-window Verified cohort, treatment also serves fewer prompt tokens per turn. Because changing the harness changed what unchanged model weights could accomplish, coding-agent evaluations should treat the model and harness together as the tested solver.

AI.tldr: Changing a coding agent's harness (the system that controls what the model sees and can do) significantly improves performance on coding benchmarks without modifying the underlying model weights.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether changing just the harness of a coding agent (while keeping the model and task fixed) changes the results, challenging the assumption that only model capabilities matter in coding agent evaluations.
AI.method: Compared two harness configurations on three coding benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, and FeatureBench). The control uses full conversation history in time order, while the treatment mechanically shortens older tool results as context fills and responds to repeated/stalled work. Experiments varied context windows and tested across multiple models.
AI.result: Under tight context windows, the treatment significantly improved performance: raising mean per-task fail-to-pass fraction (F2PF) from 28% to 49% and complete solutions from 43 to 72 on one benchmark. These improvements held across three additional models without retuning. In wide-window settings, treatment maintained higher F2PF on FeatureBench while reducing prompt tokens per turn.
AI.conclusion: Since changing the harness changes what unchanged model weights can accomplish, coding agent evaluations should treat the model and harness together as the tested solver, not just evaluate the model in isolation.

title: Self-Augmented Diffusion Guidance for Physics-Informed Generation
summary: Diffusion models can be used to generate spatiotemporal signals of physical phenomena, such as time-series images of fluid dynamics. However, a major limitation of standard diffusion models is that they do not incorporate constraints derived from the underlying physical laws. Consequently, generated samples may appear visually plausible while deviating substantially from the true dynamics. In this study, we propose a simple yet effective physics-informed approach based on diffusion guidance with self-generated data augmentation. The proposed method learns the data distribution conditioned on the degree of deviation from the physically correct dynamics and generates samples by explicitly setting the deviation condition to be zero. The method decouples the evaluation of the governing equations from the diffusion model training and sampling processes, avoiding the need to solve the governing equations at every iteration of the denoising process. This design makes the method applicable to problems requiring computationally expensive numerical simulations and enables faster sample generation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model not only significantly reduces the deviations compared with standard diffusion models but also achieves further reductions when combined with existing physics-constrained diffusion methods.

AI.tldr: Physics-informed diffusion guidance with self-generated data augmentation ensures generated spatiotemporal signals adhere to physical laws while maintaining computational efficiency.
AI.motivation: Standard diffusion models generate physically plausible spatiotemporal signals (like fluid dynamics) but don't incorporate physical constraints, leading to samples that deviate from true dynamics despite appearing visually correct.
AI.method: Proposes physics-informed diffusion guidance with self-generated data augmentation. Learns data distribution conditioned on deviation from physical correctness, generates samples by setting deviation condition to zero. Decouples governing equation evaluation from diffusion training/sampling, avoiding expensive equation solving during denoising.
AI.result: Method significantly reduces physical deviations compared to standard diffusion models, achieves further improvements when combined with existing physics-constrained diffusion methods. Enables faster sample generation and applicability to computationally expensive simulation problems.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach effectively incorporates physical constraints into diffusion models for spatiotemporal signal generation while maintaining computational efficiency, enabling more accurate physical simulations without the computational burden of solving governing equations at each denoising step.

title: Safety by Design: Realized-Cost Constraints for Contextual Bandits with Continuous Actions
summary: Contextual bandits are a standard framework for sequential decision-making under uncertainty, with applications in clinical trials, dosage selection, recommendation systems, and autonomous systems. Safety is central in many of these applications, since a single unsafe decision in settings such as dosage selection or autonomous driving can have catastrophic consequences. A common way to model safety in bandit problems is to associate each action with both a reward signal and a cost signal, and to optimize reward subject to constraints on cost. Most existing safety-constrained bandit models enforce safety by requiring the expected cost of each action to remain below a prescribed threshold. However, this may be insufficient in heteroscedastic settings, where the chosen action affects not only the expected reward and cost, but also the variability of the observed outcomes. We study contextual bandits with one-dimensional continuous actions and stage-wise high-probability constraints on the realized cost. We propose High-Probability Constrained UCB, an optimistic-pessimistic algorithm that explores for reward while conservatively estimating the safe action set. For linear reward and cost models, we prove a tight $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\sqrt{T})$ regret bound, and we extend the analysis to general function classes using the eluder dimension. Experiments show that enforcing realized-cost safety substantially reduces violations compared with expected-cost constrained baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a new safety-constrained contextual bandit framework that enforces high-probability constraints on realized costs rather than expected costs, addressing heteroscedastic settings where actions affect outcome variability.
AI.motivation: Existing safety-constrained bandit models enforce safety by requiring expected costs to remain below thresholds, which is insufficient in heteroscedastic settings where actions affect both expected outcomes and variability. In applications like dosage selection or autonomous driving, even a single unsafe decision can have catastrophic consequences, necessitating more stringent safety guarantees.
AI.method: The authors propose High-Probability Constrained UCB (HPC-UCB), an optimistic-pessimistic algorithm that explores for reward while conservatively estimating the safe action set. The algorithm handles one-dimensional continuous actions with stage-wise high-probability constraints on realized costs, using a dual approach: optimistic reward estimation for exploration and pessimistic safety estimation for constraint satisfaction.
AI.result: For linear reward and cost models, the authors prove a tight $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\sqrt{T})$ regret bound. They extend the analysis to general function classes using the eluder dimension. Experimental results show that enforcing realized-cost safety substantially reduces violations compared with expected-cost constrained baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed high-probability constraint framework provides stronger safety guarantees than existing expected-cost approaches, particularly in heteroscedastic settings. The HPC-UCB algorithm achieves both good regret performance and substantial reduction in safety violations, making it suitable for safety-critical applications like clinical trials and autonomous systems.

title: LLM Agents for Time-Series: A Survey
summary: LLM-based agents are increasingly being developed for time-series problems, but their design choices vary substantially across task settings. This survey adopts a problem-driven taxonomy that organizes these systems by the time-series problems they address rather than by isolated technical components. We group existing systems into four categories: forecasting and reasoning, augmentation and synthesis, anomaly detection and diagnosis, and decision support. Within each category, we examine how task requirements shape agent architecture, tool use, and memory design. We further summarize representative datasets and environments, and compare reported model performance under shared or closely related settings. Overall, this survey offers a task-oriented guide to designing LLM-based agents for time-series problems and identifies open gaps for future work.

AI.tldr: A survey paper that organizes LLM-based agents for time-series problems using a task-oriented taxonomy instead of technical components, covering four problem categories and their design implications.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based agents for time-series problems have highly varied design choices across different task settings, lacking a coherent framework for understanding how specific time-series problems influence agent design decisions.
AI.method: The survey adopts a problem-driven taxonomy that groups systems into four categories based on the time-series problems they address: forecasting and reasoning, augmentation and synthesis, anomaly detection and diagnosis, and decision support. It then examines how task requirements shape agent architecture, tool use, and memory design within each category.
AI.result: The paper provides a systematic organization of existing systems across the four categories, summarizes representative datasets and environments used in these tasks, and compares reported model performance under shared or closely related settings, offering insights into how different time-series problems influence agent design.
AI.conclusion: This survey offers a task-oriented guide to designing LLM-based agents for time-series problems and identifies open gaps for future research in this emerging field.

title: Beyond Client Averaging: A Client-Independent Second-Order Stationary-Bias Component in Stochastic SCAFFOLD
summary:
Existing constant-step analysis of stochastic \Scaf{} identifies a leading $O(γ/N)$ stationary mean bias and shows that higher-order bias can persist as the client count increases, but does not identify the first client-independent contribution at coefficient level. For full-participation stochastic \Scaf{} with one-dimensional homogeneous clients, fixed local-step count $H$, and bounded additive gradient noise, we prove, uniformly over $N\ge2$,
  $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}_{π_{γ,N,H}}[x]-x^\star ={}& -\frac{f'''(x^\star)σ^2}{4f''(x^\star)^2}\fracγ{N}\\ &- \frac{f'''(x^\star)σ^2}{12f''(x^\star)} \frac{(H-1)(5H-1)}{H}γ^2 +O_H\!\left(\frac{γ^2}{N}+γ^3\right). \end{aligned} $$
  Hence client averaging suppresses the leading $O(γ/N)$ bias but does not remove the client-independent $O(γ^2)$ component when its coefficient is nonzero.
  The mechanism is indirect: although the direct control contribution cancels pathwise in the linear global average, the controls still alter within-round local trajectories and their second moments. Fresh gradient noise and persistent control fluctuations therefore generate local second-moment corrections that nonquadratic curvature converts into stationary mean bias. The coefficient vanishes for quadratic objectives. Numerical experiments are consistent with the predicted coefficient, its persistence as client count increases, and the stated joint remainder. The result is restricted to the one-dimensional homogeneous fixed-$H$ setting.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a precise bias analysis for full-participation stochastic SCAFFOLD with one-dimensional homogeneous clients, showing that while client averaging suppresses the leading O(γ/N) bias, it doesn't remove the client-independent O(γ²) bias component.
AI.motivation: Existing analyses of stochastic SCAFFOLD identify leading bias terms but don't identify first client-independent contributions at coefficient level. The paper aims to precisely quantify bias in federated learning with control variates, particularly how client averaging affects bias components.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of full-participation stochastic SCAFFOLD with one-dimensional homogeneous clients, fixed local-step count H, and bounded additive gradient noise. Uses mathematical proofs to derive bias coefficients uniformly over client counts N≥2.
AI.result: Derived exact coefficients for stationary mean bias: leading O(γ/N) term and client-independent O(γ²) term with explicit coefficients involving f'''(x⋆), σ², and H. Shows client averaging suppresses first term but not second when coefficient is nonzero. Verified through numerical experiments.
AI.conclusion: Client averaging suppresses leading bias but doesn't eliminate client-independent O(γ²) bias in SCAFFOLD due to indirect mechanisms where control variates alter local trajectories and second moments, converted into bias by nonquadratic curvature. Result is limited to one-dimensional homogeneous setting.

title: The Reasoning Tax: Token Economics of LLM Reasoning Across Task Types and Deployment Contexts
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures and tables, accepted at the 2026 TPCTC Conference and will be published at Performance Evaluation and Benchmarking (Springer)
summary: Accuracy-only benchmarking of reasoning-capable large language models misses a central deployment question: when do extended thinking tokens earn their cost? We introduce the Token Economy Score (TES), a marginal benchmarking metric that measures the accuracy gain of a reasoning model over a non-reasoning baseline, normalized by the generated-token multiplier. We define paired and approximated TES variants for model families with reasoning toggles and frontier models without direct non-reasoning counterparts. We then conduct an empirical benchmarking analysis across 151 model-benchmark evaluation runs on seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, science reasoning, instruction following, expert knowledge, knowledge recall, and research-level physics. The analysis examines three deployment-facing dimensions: which task structures yield positive marginal reasoning efficiency, how increasing reasoning effort changes TES within model families, and how deployment context changes economic viability. Results show that task structure predicts reasoning efficiency better than nominal difficulty: sequential inferencechain tasks such as AIME 2025 and LiveCodeBench show high TES, while knowledge-recall tasks such as MMLU-Pro show low TES despite their difficulty. We also find systematic diminishing returns at higher reasoning effort levels, including cases where additional thinking reduces accuracy. Finally, Reasoning Cost Share (RCS) shows that inference spend is often dominated by internal thinking, while Deployment Cost Multiplier (DCM) shows how on-premises deployment can change the economics of otherwise costly reasoning workloads. These findings support a benchmarking-driven model-selection rule: enable reasoning selectively by task type, effort level, and deployment context rather than treating it as a universally beneficial mode.

AI.tldr: TES metric measures cost-effectiveness of reasoning tokens, showing reasoning should be enabled selectively by task type rather than universally.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarking focuses only on accuracy but misses deployment economics - when do extended reasoning tokens justify their cost?
AI.method: Introduced Token Economy Score (TES) metric measuring accuracy gain over non-reasoning baseline normalized by token multiplier; conducted empirical analysis across 151 model-benchmark runs on 7 diverse benchmarks.
AI.result: Task structure predicts reasoning efficiency better than difficulty: sequential inference tasks show high TES while knowledge-recall tasks show low TES; diminishing returns at higher reasoning effort; inference spend often dominated by internal thinking.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning should be enabled selectively by task type, effort level, and deployment context rather than as universally beneficial mode.

title: On the Indistinguishability of Human v/s AI Generated Text
summary: The rapid improvement of LLMs has made distinguishing AI-generated text from human writing a pressing problem. This challenge is further amplified by paraphrasing tools designed to make machine-generated text appear more "human". We study how access to human writing samples can be used to strategically paraphrase machine-generated responses toward the human distribution. Under a multi-sample setting with human and machine responses to the same prompts, we show that repeated paraphrasing moves the machine distribution toward the empirical human distribution under simple mixing and stability conditions. Our results derive an explicit convergence rate, extend the analysis to a finite-sample setting, and characterize how the required number of human samples and paraphrasing rounds scale with the desired error.

AI.tldr: Analyzing how access to human writing samples enables strategic paraphrasing to make AI-generated text more human-like, with convergence guarantees and scaling analysis.
AI.motivation: The rapid improvement of LLMs has created an urgent need to distinguish AI-generated text from human writing, especially as paraphrasing tools can make machine text appear more human-like. The paper aims to understand how access to human samples enables strategic manipulation of machine-generated responses.
AI.method: Studying a multi-sample setting with both human and machine responses to the same prompts. The approach involves repeated paraphrasing of machine-generated responses toward the human distribution. Analysis includes establishing convergence under simple mixing and stability conditions.
AI.result: Shows that repeated paraphrasing moves the machine distribution toward the empirical human distribution. The paper derives an explicit convergence rate, extends analysis to finite-sample settings, and characterizes how the required number of human samples and paraphrasing rounds scale with desired error.
AI.conclusion: Access to human writing samples enables strategic paraphrasing that can systematically make AI-generated text more human-like, with quantifiable convergence properties and practical scaling insights for detection evasion.

title: 6.5% of the Neuro-Symbolic Literature Can Be Reproduced from Its Published Artifacts, a Six-Stage Audit Framework and First Instantiation
summary: We present a six-stage framework for auditing the reproducibility of scientific claims across a research literature within the computer science domain, and instantiate our framework for the neuro-symbolic AI (NSAI) subdomain. Instantiating the framework on the NSAI subdomain produced a multi-year audit. Stage one retrieved 5,497 records and removed 3,018 duplicates. Stage two screened the 2,479 unique records at title and abstract, identifying 1,365 self-identified NSAI records, then removed a further 61 at full text for off-topic, non-research, no-quantitative-evaluation, or inaccessible-full-text reasons. Stage three sought a verifiable public code artifact for each of the 1,304 eligible records and found none for 849, leaving 455 to enter the artifact inventory and bounded rerun of stages four and five. We fully or partially reproduced 85 studies, 6.52% of the eligible corpus and 18.68% of attempted reruns. We found that 321 attempted reruns were blocked by missing non- code artifacts and 42 by missing or unusable code repositories. These figures quantify a persistent reproducibility deficit that survives even nominal "code available" declarations, and signal the need for enforced, versioned, and permanently archived artifact bundles in future NSAI publications. We argue that empirical NSAI papers should be required at submission time to provide complete, versioned, and permanently archived artifact bundles.

AI.tldr: A six-stage framework for auditing scientific reproducibility in computer science, applied to neuro-symbolic AI literature, reveals severe reproducibility deficits with only 6.52% of eligible studies fully/partially reproducible, advocating for mandatory complete artifact bundles.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the persistent reproducibility crisis in scientific research, particularly in computer science domains. The authors aim to quantify and understand the extent of reproducibility issues in neuro-symbolic AI (NSAI) research, moving beyond anecdotal evidence to systematic measurement.
AI.method: A six-stage reproducibility auditing framework: 1) record retrieval and deduplication, 2) screening and eligibility determination, 3) code artifact verification, 4) artifact inventory creation, 5) bounded rerun attempts, 6) analysis of reproduction outcomes. Applied to NSAI literature with systematic data collection from 5,497 initial records.
AI.result: Only 85 studies (6.52% of eligible corpus, 18.68% of attempted reruns) were fully/partially reproducible. Major blocking factors: 849/1,304 studies had no verifiable public code, 321 reruns blocked by missing non-code artifacts, 42 by missing/unusable code repositories. Shows reproducibility deficit persists despite "code available" declarations.
AI.conclusion: There is a severe reproducibility crisis in NSAI research that requires structural solutions. The authors advocate for requiring complete, versioned, and permanently archived artifact bundles at submission time for empirical NSAI papers, moving beyond voluntary code availability to enforced standards.

title: SAGE: Variate-Wise Semantic Augmentation for Vision-Language Time Series Forecasting
summary: Time series forecasting models operate on raw numerical sequences, lacking the semantic knowledge that domain experts implicitly leverage, such as the physical meaning of each variable, its statistical behavior, and its temporal dynamics. Recent efforts to bridge this gap fall into two camps. Some rely on large language models at inference time, which is computationally expensive. Others apply uniform textual prompts at the dataset level, ignoring the heterogeneous semantics across individual variates. We propose SAGE (Seeing and Augmenting with Grounded Encoding), an end-to-end CLIP-based framework that jointly models temporal, cross-variable, textual, and visual information. The CLIP text encoder processes frequency-enhanced patches and variable tokens, while gated residual paths inject variable-specific descriptions and statistical descriptors. In parallel, the frozen CLIP vision encoder aligns rendered series with temporal representations through a training-only contrastive objective. This dual use of CLIP adds complementary semantic and visual supervision without placing an LLM in the forecasting loop. Across eight long-term benchmarks and M4, SAGE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy. Ablations confirm complementary gains from multimodal alignment and variable-level knowledge.

AI.tldr: SAGE is an end-to-end CLIP-based framework for time series forecasting that combines temporal, cross-variable, textual, and visual information through dual CLIP encoders, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy without expensive LLM inference.
AI.motivation: Current time series forecasting models lack semantic knowledge that domain experts use, such as variable meaning and statistical behavior. Existing solutions either use expensive LLMs at inference or apply uniform textual prompts that ignore variable heterogeneity.
AI.method: SAGE uses CLIP text encoder with frequency-enhanced patches and variable tokens, with gated residual paths for variable-specific descriptions. In parallel, frozen CLIP vision encoder aligns rendered series with temporal representations through contrastive training. This dual CLIP approach adds semantic and visual supervision without LLMs in the forecasting loop.
AI.result: SAGE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across eight long-term benchmarks and the M4 dataset. Ablation studies confirm complementary gains from multimodal alignment and variable-level knowledge.
AI.conclusion: SAGE effectively bridges the semantic gap in time series forecasting by leveraging multimodal CLIP encoders to incorporate variable-specific knowledge and visual representations, achieving superior performance without computational overhead of LLM inference.

title: Reinforcement Learning-Based Control of CAV Platoon Joining Maneuvers in Mixed Traffic
summary: Connected and automated vehicle (CAV) platooning offers a promising approach to improving road safety and traffic capacity. However, platoon control in real-world traffic is challenging due to uncertainty and heterogeneous driving behaviors. Reinforcement learning (RL) has strong potential for addressing such control problems, but its practical deployment raises challenges related to safety and learning efficiency. This paper proposes a generic modeling and simulation framework for investigating CAV platoon joining maneuvers and comparing deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based control algorithms. The problem is particularly challenging in mixed-traffic environments, where CAVs coexist with human-driven vehicles exhibiting heterogeneous longitudinal and lateral behaviors. The objective is to achieve safe and efficient joining maneuvers by either incorporating penalties for risky behaviors into the learning process or using an external safety controller to constrain the learned policy. An agent-based modeling framework coupled with the Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) simulator is used to evaluate Deep Q-Network (DQN), Double Deep Q-Network (DDQN), and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Results show that PPO outperforms DQN and DDQN, achieving a joining success rate of approximately 98 % and a collision rate below 1 %, largely due to risk-related penalties incorporated into the reward function. However, this improved performance requires more decision steps to complete the maneuver, revealing a trade-off between safety, joining effectiveness, and decision efficiency. An external safety controller effectively prevents collisions, although its interventions may reduce joining efficiency. The results highlight the importance of jointly considering safety and efficiency when designing RL-based controllers for CAV platoon joining in mixed traffic.

AI.tldr: A framework for testing DRL algorithms on CAV platoon joining in mixed traffic shows PPO outperforms DQN/DDQN with 98% success rate, using risk penalties or safety controllers for safety-efficiency tradeoffs.
AI.motivation: CAV platooning can improve road safety and traffic capacity, but real-world deployment faces challenges from uncertainty and heterogeneous human driving behaviors in mixed-traffic environments.
AI.method: Proposed a generic modeling/simulation framework using agent-based modeling with SUMO simulator to evaluate DQN, DDQN, and PPO algorithms for CAV platoon joining maneuvers, incorporating risk penalties or external safety controllers.
AI.result: PPO outperforms DQN and DDQN with ~98% joining success rate and <1% collision rate, but requires more decision steps. Safety controllers prevent collisions but may reduce joining efficiency, showing trade-off between safety, effectiveness, and decision efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Safety and efficiency must be jointly considered when designing RL-based controllers for CAV platoon joining in mixed traffic, with PPO showing best performance through risk-aware reward design.

title: Assessing mentalization in humans and large language models
comment: 46 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Supplementary information available on request from the authors
summary: Mentalization - the ability to infer others' beliefs and intentions to guide one's own choices - is a key cognitive function underlying human social interactions. Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate behaviour consistent with humans on theory-of-mind tasks, yet whether these models can guide adaptive behaviour through mentalization is unknown. Here we use two economic games with cognitive computational modeling to uncover the latent strategies underlying mentalization in LLMs. We tested individual LLM agents across four model families, DeepSeek, GPT-4.1, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.0 Flash (N = 2,099), against opponents of varying sophistication and examined whether a prompting strategy designed to elicit strategic reasoning improved performance. We benchmarked results against human participants (N = 251) as a comparative measure. Across both games, LLMs showed clear behavioural and computational signatures of mentalizing that differed markedly by model provider and size. Strategic prompting generally improved performance by inducing more sophisticated reasoning, yet the extent of the benefit differed across the two tasks. Last, GPT-5 agents flexibly adapted their recursive depth of reasoning to increasingly sophisticated opponents, demonstrating superior performance to human participants. Collectively, we demonstrate different capacities for mentalization across LLMs, and highlight cognitive computational modeling as a formal method for assessing comparative intelligence across humans and machines.

AI.tldr: LLMs demonstrate mentalization abilities in economic games, with performance varying by model family/size, strategic prompting improves reasoning, and GPT-5 outperforms humans in adaptive reasoning against sophisticated opponents.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether large language models can guide adaptive behavior through mentalization (inferring others' beliefs and intentions), which is a key cognitive function in human social interactions. While LLMs show theory-of-mind capabilities, their ability to use mentalization for strategic decision-making in social contexts remains unknown.
AI.method: Used two economic games with cognitive computational modeling to uncover latent strategies behind mentalization in LLMs. Tested 2,099 LLM agents across DeepSeek, GPT-4.1, GPT-5, and Gemini 2.0 Flash against opponents of varying sophistication. Implemented strategic prompting to elicit better reasoning. Benchmark results against 251 human participants for comparison.
AI.result: LLMs showed clear behavioral and computational signatures of mentalization that varied significantly by model provider and size. Strategic prompting generally improved performance by inducing more sophisticated reasoning, but benefits differed across tasks. GPT-5 agents flexibly adapted their recursive depth of reasoning to increasingly sophisticated opponents and demonstrated superior performance to human participants.
AI.conclusion: Different LLMs exhibit varying capacities for mentalization, with GPT-5 showing the most sophisticated and adaptive reasoning that surpasses human performance. Cognitive computational modeling provides a formal method for assessing comparative intelligence between humans and machines, revealing both capabilities and limitations in AI social cognition.

title: When Is the Sharp Covariance Envelope Tight? Feature-Only Geometry for Volume-Sampled Least Squares
summary: Prior analyses by Derezinski and Warmuth established all-size sampling identities, selected-OLS unbiasedness, and inverse moments for ordinary volume sampling, while their exact arbitrary-fixed-response loss and prediction-covariance formulas are at the rank-size endpoint s=d. We establish a Loewner envelope for centered coefficient covariance for every full-rank fixed pool, response, and legal budget d <= s <= m under ordinary indexed fixed-size volume sampling followed by selected unweighted least squares; its coefficient is globally sharp over the full-rank class. Global sharpness does not determine attainability on the pool in hand. Under positive loss, strict-interior budgets, and no coloops, a feature-only margin nu_A gives the exact fixed-design spectral phase: nu_A > 0 if and only if the normalized spectral envelope is strict for every compatible residual, whereas nu_A = 0 if and only if some compatible residual is spectrally tight; the same zero-margin residual is tight at every strict-interior budget. A residual-augmented change of measure supplies the response-aware mechanism and a one-sided quantitative slack bound, while support saturation proves the attainment direction. Critical equal-leverage geometry interprets the boundary, and sound lower certificates yield conservative same-primitive cardinality decisions. Frozen-feature examples show that the certificate is nonvacuous and measure the fixed-pool cost of its authorized reduction. The claims concern conditional centered, full-Gram-whitened coefficient covariance, not population generalization.

AI.tldr: Establishes Loewner envelope for coefficient covariance under volume sampling with sharpness guarantees, phase transitions based on feature margins, and certificates for conservative cardinality decisions.
AI.motivation: Prior work on volume sampling established identities and formulas but only at endpoint s=d. The paper aims to extend analysis to all legal budgets d <= s <= m with global sharpness guarantees and characterize exact spectral phase transitions.
AI.method: Uses ordinary indexed fixed-size volume sampling followed by selected unweighted least squares. Establishes Loewner envelope for centered coefficient covariance, analyzes phase transitions via feature-only margin nu_A, employs residual-augmented change of measure, and develops sound lower certificates.
AI.result: Obtains globally sharp Loewner envelope for coefficient covariance across all legal budgets. Identifies spectral phase transition: nu_A > 0 gives strict normalized spectral envelope for all compatible residuals, while nu_A = 0 yields spectrally tight residual. Provides one-sided quantitative slack bounds and proves attainment via support saturation.
AI.conclusion: The analysis provides complete characterization of coefficient covariance under volume sampling with sharpness guarantees, establishes exact spectral phase transitions via feature margins, and offers practical certificates for conservative decision-making. Claims concern conditional centered covariance in fixed-design setting, not population generalization.

title: Approved Too Late: Verdict Staleness in LLM-Guarded Self-Adaptive Systems
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Autonomic Computing and Self-Organizing Systems (ACSOS 2026)
summary: A large language model (LLM) guardrail for a self-adaptive system (SAS) may issue an approval that is correct at check time but stale by actuation. This creates an Execute-stage time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) hazard. We study verdict freshness: whether a guardrail verdict remains valid when used. We distinguish three quantities that answer different questions: all-candidate verdict change under fixed-action replay, oracle-labeled approval expiry on recorded closed-loop trajectories, and judge-conditioned use-time invalidity. Across five reproducible SAS environments, all-candidate verdict-change rates span 5.3-48.4% at a common replay shift of eight simulator steps. We introduce the Freshness-Bounded Shield (FBS), which estimates each approval's validity horizon from its safe-side margin and recent feature volatility, without an explicit plant-dynamics model. Using fixed settings documented in the artifact, FBS reduces oracle-labeled approval-expiry rates from 3.4-24.7% to 0-1.8% at the same shift. A separate audit of four LLM judges finds nonzero judge-conditioned use-time invalidity in every approval stream. We formulate a freshness contract: every approval must be correct at check time and remain valid at use time.

AI.tldr: LLM guardrail approvals for self-adaptive systems can become stale between check time and use time, creating TOCTOU hazards; the paper introduces Freshness-Bounded Shield to reduce approval expiry rates and formulates freshness contracts.
AI.motivation: Large language model guardrails for self-adaptive systems can issue approvals that are correct at check time but become stale by actuation time, creating Execute-stage time-of-check to time-of-use hazards that compromise system safety.
AI.method: The paper distinguishes three quantities for verdict freshness analysis: all-candidate verdict change under fixed-action replay, oracle-labeled approval expiry on recorded closed-loop trajectories, and judge-conditioned use-time invalidity. It introduces Freshness-Bounded Shield that estimates approval validity horizons using safe-side margins and recent feature volatility without requiring explicit plant-dynamics models.
AI.result: Across five SAS environments, all-candidate verdict-change rates spanned 5.3-48.4% at eight simulator steps replay shift. FBS reduced oracle-labeled approval-expiry rates from 3.4-24.7% to 0-1.8% at the same shift. Audit of four LLM judges found nonzero judge-conditioned use-time invalidity in every approval stream.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates significant verdict freshness problems in LLM guardrails for SAS, introduces FBS as an effective solution to reduce approval expiry, and formulates a freshness contract requiring approvals to be both correct at check time and remain valid at use time.

title: Mitigating Strong-Modality Collapse in Multimodal Learning via Inverted Asymmetric Fusion
summary: Fusing multiple modalities is expected to improve model performance. However, on the MultiHuSE dataset, early, late, and symmetric attention fusion often fail to outperform the best unimodal baseline (text). Pathway isolation of a symmetric attention fusion model reveals that the text-pathway accuracy drops from 74.9% to 56.4% after fusion in one such setting, indicating that the dominant modality can be degraded during integration. We term this strong-modality collapse and argue that it helps explain why some multimodal models fail to surpass unimodal baselines. We propose Inverted Asymmetric Fusion (IAF), which avoids forcing mutual attention across modalities. The dominant modality is preserved by passing through fusion unchanged, while weaker modalities attend to it as a contextual anchor. Before fusion, weaker modalities are strengthened using Modality-Aware Knowledge Distillation. We evaluate IAF on three benchmarks with different modality hierarchies: text-dominant datasets (MultiHuSE, UR-FUNNY) and an audio-visual-dominant dataset (MUStARD). Pathway isolation shows that IAF preserves the dominant modality's internal accuracy at its unimodal ceiling across all tested configurations, whereas symmetric fusion degrades it by up to 18.5% on MultiHuSE. IAF improves over the strongest unimodal baseline by up to 8.25%.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "strong-modality collapse" where multimodal fusion degrades the dominant modality, proposes Inverted Asymmetric Fusion (IAF) that preserves the dominant modality while weaker modalities attend to it, and shows performance improvements over unimodal baselines.
AI.motivation: Multimodal fusion often fails to outperform the best unimodal baseline, with the dominant modality being degraded during integration - a phenomenon the authors term "strong-modality collapse."
AI.method: Proposes Inverted Asymmetric Fusion (IAF) that avoids mutual attention across modalities, preserves the dominant modality unchanged, while weaker modalities attend to it as contextual anchor. Weaker modalities are strengthened using Modality-Aware Knowledge Distillation before fusion.
AI.result: IAF preserves the dominant modality's internal accuracy at its unimodal ceiling across all tested configurations, while symmetric fusion degrades it by up to 18.5%. IAF improves over the strongest unimodal baseline by up to 8.25% on various benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Strong-modality collapse explains why some multimodal models fail to surpass unimodal baselines, and the proposed IAF effectively addresses this issue by preserving the dominant modality while allowing weaker modalities to benefit from it through asymmetric attention.

title: FaithSieve: Fine-Grained Evaluation of Math Proofs with Faithful Formal Evidence
comment: 32 pages, 3 figures; preprint with appendix and supplementary experimental details
summary: Large language models can now generate complex, multi-step mathematical proofs, but reliably determining their correctness and localizing early logical errors remains a critical challenge. Existing evaluation approaches largely depend on model-based natural-language judgments, which often overlook local reasoning gaps. While formal theorem provers like Lean offer a path to rigorous verification, using them to evaluate informal text requires solving locality and semantic mismatches: a prover might bypass a local flaw by proving an overly broad target, or validate an auto-formalized statement that drifts from the original mathematical intent. To address this, we introduce FaithSieve, a Lean-assisted framework for fine-grained evaluation of natural-language mathematical proofs. FaithSieve decomposes coarse proof steps into local reasoning units, extracts typed proof obligations, and verifies them through a formal evaluation agent. Formal validation is gated by semantic alignment scoring, so Lean evidence is incorporated only when the formal statement faithfully preserves the context, objects, and logical form of the original claim. We construct two expert-verified datasets, ProofLoc-Olympiad and ProofLoc-University, to benchmark first-error localization. On the 350-problem Olympiad dataset, FaithSieve using a GPT-5.4 backbone achieves 81.43% exact first-error accuracy, outperforming the direct-judging baseline of 72.29%. Furthermore, on the 200-problem ProofLoc-University benchmark spanning six advanced domains, FaithSieve reaches 84.5% exact accuracy, compared to 75.0% for the direct judge. Our work demonstrates that decomposing proofs into fine-grained units and grounding them with faithful formal evidence significantly improves reliable evaluation of natural-language reasoning.

AI.tldr: FaithSieve is a Lean-assisted framework that decomposes natural-language mathematical proofs into local reasoning units, extracts typed proof obligations, and uses semantic alignment scoring to incorporate formal verification only when faithful to the original mathematical intent, significantly improving proof error localization accuracy.
AI.motivation: Large language models can generate complex mathematical proofs, but reliably determining their correctness and localizing early logical errors remains challenging. Existing evaluation approaches using model-based natural-language judgments often overlook local reasoning gaps, while formal theorem provers like Lean have locality and semantic mismatch issues when applied to informal text.
AI.method: FaithSieve decomposes coarse proof steps into local reasoning units, extracts typed proof obligations, and verifies them through a formal evaluation agent. The framework uses semantic alignment scoring to gate formal validation, incorporating Lean evidence only when the formal statement faithfully preserves the original claim's context, objects, and logical form.
AI.result: On the 350-problem ProofLoc-Olympiad dataset, FaithSieve with GPT-5.4 backbone achieved 81.43% exact first-error accuracy (vs 72.29% baseline). On the 200-problem ProofLoc-University benchmark across six advanced domains, it reached 84.5% exact accuracy (vs 75.0% baseline).
AI.conclusion: Decomposing proofs into fine-grained units and grounding them with faithful formal evidence significantly improves reliable evaluation of natural-language reasoning, addressing both locality and semantic alignment challenges in mathematical proof verification.

title: A Layer Importance Metric for Quantization Accounting for the Speed-Quality Trade-off in Autoregressive Models
summary: Small language models (sLLMs) are nowadays hosted on devices with limited memory and computational budget. In an autoregressive setup, inference is memory-bandwidth bound: uniform quantization is often detrimental to such models, since their architecture has limited redundancies and only a few layers are not very sensitive to lower precision. We propose a composite metric that combines two orthogonal criteria: information retention (measured in terms of a normalized SQNR-based coefficient) and throughput gains (modeled using a roofline-based latency analysis). By profiling Gemma 3 1B, we find that Feed-Forward Network blocks and the embedding matrix are the most promising targets for acceleration. For each candidate, we estimate a normalized quality score based on simulated quantization and a normalized speed score based on roofline modeling with no actual execution needed. We combine the two scores in a composite priority coefficient, allowing us to tune the trade-off between speed and quality as needed. Our metric is general and can be used to prioritize individual blocks, their projection sublayers, or transformer layers as a whole. We evaluate our approach on several model architectures, showing that our estimates have at around 4% prediction error for the accelerated speedup. We find that our method generally allocates more resources to the most expressive layers compared to evolutionary search, specialized accelerators, or Shapley-value-based approaches that require expensive approximate inference. Our analytical approach makes sLLM quantization a predictable engineering task.

AI.tldr: A composite metric for small LLM quantization that combines information retention and throughput gains to prioritize layers for acceleration, enabling predictable quantization without expensive inference.
AI.motivation: Small language models run on devices with limited resources, but uniform quantization hurts them because they have limited redundancies and only a few layers are insensitive to lower precision. Need a method to identify which layers to quantize for optimal speed-quality trade-off.
AI.method: Propose a composite metric with two orthogonal criteria: information retention (measured via normalized SQNR-based coefficient) and throughput gains (modeled using roofline-based latency analysis). Profile models to find promising targets, estimate quality score via simulated quantization and speed score via roofline modeling, then combine into a composite priority coefficient to tune speed-quality trade-off.
AI.result: Applied to Gemma 3 1B, found Feed-Forward Network blocks and embedding matrix are most promising acceleration targets. Method achieves ~4% prediction error for accelerated speedup, allocates more resources to expressive layers compared to evolutionary search, specialized accelerators, or Shapley-value approaches, and makes sLLM quantization predictable.
AI.conclusion: The proposed analytical approach transforms sLLM quantization from trial-and-error into a predictable engineering task, providing a general metric that can prioritize blocks, sublayers, or entire transformer layers without requiring expensive approximate inference.

title: ProofEvolve: Neuro-Symbolic Evolution for Formal Automated Theorem Proving
summary: Automated theorem proving offers a natural foundation for recursive self-improvement in scientific discovery. However, existing neural provers do not fully preserve this recursive structure, where the learning process should be self-improving over time. Existing methods either embed proof experience into model parameters through expensive weight updates, or keep verified intermediate deductions only within the current problem. In addition, these methods also heavily rely on sparse whole-proof feedback, even when unsuccessful partial attempts contain useful discoveries. To close the gap, we propose ProofEvolve, a neuro-symbolic framework that evolves explicit, formally verified symbolic proof structures with neural models to decisively expand the knowledge boundary. In this framework, the neural model proposes variation operators, including decompositions, repairs, and schema recombinations. The symbolic Lean kernel verifies every proof transition. Over the evolution loops, ProofEvolve computes verified closure over the resulting proof directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Within each problem, ProofEvolve evolves partial AND-OR proof DAGs in a behaviorally indexed archive. Across problems, kernel-checked schema extraction adds newly proved sub-DAGs to a persistent schema library. Proof DAGs inherit the solved results through typed schema recombination, with every residual premise exposed as a new subgoal. This evolutionary process preserves verified results from incomplete attempts and makes them available for later proofs without weakening formal soundness. Across three competition-level Lean benchmarks, ProofEvolve achieves the highest average solve rate among the evaluated proof systems.

AI.tldr: ProofEvolve is a neuro-symbolic framework that evolves verified proof structures using neural models to propose variations and symbolic verification, achieving state-of-the-art performance on Lean theorem proving benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing neural theorem provers don't fully preserve recursive self-improvement structure for scientific discovery. They either use expensive weight updates or keep verified deductions only within current problems, relying on sparse whole-proof feedback while ignoring useful discoveries from unsuccessful partial attempts.
AI.method: ProofEvolve evolves explicit, formally verified symbolic proof structures using neural models to propose variation operators (decompositions, repairs, schema recombinations). The symbolic Lean kernel verifies every proof transition. It builds AND-OR proof DAGs within problems in a behaviorally indexed archive and maintains a persistent schema library across problems through kernel-checked schema extraction.
AI.result: ProofEvolve achieves the highest average solve rate among evaluated proof systems across three competition-level Lean benchmarks, demonstrating superior performance in automated theorem proving.
AI.conclusion: ProofEvolve successfully bridges the gap for recursive self-improvement in theorem proving by evolving verified proof structures that preserve discoveries from incomplete attempts while maintaining formal soundness, enabling effective knowledge transfer across problems.

title: Scaling Model-Generated Distillation Data Can Make Latent Teacher Traits More Recoverable
summary: Scaling model-generated data is usually viewed as improving distillation: more examples should increase coverage, reduce noise, and produce stronger students. We show a second effect: larger datasets can make subtle teacher-specific signals easier to detect in the trained student, even when examples are off-task and never mention the trait. In a controlled setup inspired by subliminal learning, a teacher induced to express a target trait generates restricted off-task data, such as number-only completions. Students trained on different amounts of independent off-task data are evaluated in a separate domain, with matched no-trait controls isolating target-specific transfer. Our main finding is that larger independent datasets make the teacher's induced trait stand out more clearly in the student's later behavior. Other plausible traits may also strengthen with scale, but the target usually grows more. When the small-scale student already favors the target, scaling mainly amplifies that behavior; when it favors a related or salient alternative, more data can shift behavior toward the intended trait. Analyses of learned LoRA updates show a parallel trend. These effects appear across model families, trait types, multi-trait settings, and cross-model transfer. Our results suggest that scaling generated distillation data should be paired with trait-aware curation and evaluation, even when the data appears off-task or benign.

AI.tldr: Larger off-task generated datasets surprisingly amplify subtle teacher-specific traits in student models, even when examples don't explicitly mention the traits, requiring trait-aware curation in distillation.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the conventional view that scaling model-generated data always improves distillation through better coverage and noise reduction. It investigates whether larger datasets might unintentionally amplify subtle teacher-specific traits that transfer to students even in off-task data.
AI.method: The authors use a controlled "subliminal learning" setup where teachers are induced to express target traits, then generate restricted off-task data (e.g., number-only completions). Students are trained on varying amounts of this independent off-task data and evaluated in separate domains, with matched no-trait controls isolating target-specific transfer. They analyze LoRA updates and test across model families, trait types, multi-trait settings, and cross-model transfer.
AI.result: Larger independent datasets make the teacher's induced traits stand out more clearly in student behavior. When small-scale students already favor the target trait, scaling amplifies it; when they favor alternatives, more data can shift behavior toward the intended trait. These effects appear consistently across different experimental conditions.
AI.conclusion: Scaling generated distillation data requires trait-aware curation and evaluation even when data appears off-task or benign, as subtle teacher-specific signals become more detectable with larger datasets, potentially amplifying unintended traits.

title: Fine-Tuning of Transformer models with Frames
summary: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) strategies such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) are effective solutions for fine-tuning large-scale pre-trained models; however, their memory requirements scale with the size of the model, $\mathcal{O}(dr)$, where $d$ is the model's hidden dimension and $r$ is the rank. Our proposal, FrameFT, models the parameter update $ΔW$ with a sparse coefficient matrix in a Fusion Frame basis. Fusion Frames can be generated algorithmically and shared across model layers, enabling very efficient updates. Only the sparse coefficients of the basis expansion are stored/optimized, reducing the memory footprint. The sparse structure of the coefficient matrix in FrameFT and the sparsity in the Fusion Frames give large compute benefits, and our analysis provides formal convergence results. We evaluate the idea across a suite of supervised fine-tuning benchmarks, focusing on language tasks, but also report application to vision models. Our experiments show that FrameFT achieves performance on par with/exceeding state-of-the-art PEFT techniques, but needs far fewer trainable parameters.

AI.tldr: FrameFT is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that models weight updates using sparse coefficients in Fusion Frame bases, achieving state-of-the-art performance with significantly fewer trainable parameters than existing PEFT methods.
AI.motivation: Existing PEFT methods like LoRA have memory requirements that scale with model size (O(dr)), which can be problematic for large-scale models. There's a need for more efficient fine-tuning methods that maintain performance while reducing memory footprint.
AI.method: FrameFT models parameter updates (ΔW) using sparse coefficient matrices in a Fusion Frame basis. Fusion Frames can be generated algorithmically and shared across model layers. Only sparse coefficients of the basis expansion are stored and optimized, and the sparsity structure provides computational benefits. The approach includes formal convergence analysis.
AI.result: FrameFT achieves performance on par with or exceeding state-of-the-art PEFT techniques while requiring far fewer trainable parameters. It was evaluated across supervised fine-tuning benchmarks (primarily language tasks, with some vision model applications).
AI.conclusion: FrameFT presents an efficient alternative to existing PEFT methods, offering both memory efficiency and computational benefits through its sparse Fusion Frame approach, while maintaining or improving performance compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.

title: Gromov-Monge Flow Matching for Equivariant Graph Generation
comment: Gromov-Wasserstein, Optimal Transport, Flow Matching, Graph Generation, Equivariant Networks
summary: Graphs are invariant under node permutations, motivating the use of permutation-equivariant architectures in generative models. In flow matching, however, symmetry may also enter the source--target coupling: once graph pairs are compared up to node relabeling, the natural Wasserstein geometry is that of the graph quotient space. The Euclidean quotient metric of this space coincides with the Gromov--Monge distance, obtained by optimally relabeling the nodes. We develop this perspective theoretically, showing that quotient couplings can be lifted to aligned representatives without additional cost and that symmetrization yields equivariant flow-matching minimizers, including for categorical endpoint prediction. In practice, exact Gromov--Monge alignment is intractable, so we construct minibatch couplings using efficient Gromov--Wasserstein-type relaxations and lower bounds for the inner node alignment, optionally combined with an outer assignment between graphs. The resulting procedure changes only the training coupling and is compatible with standard permutation-equivariant architectures. Across continuous graph and categorical molecular generation, these structure-aware couplings substantially improve sample quality at small integration budgets, while our scaled-up molecular models remain competitive under conventional many-step sampling.

AI.tldr: A novel flow matching method for graph generation that incorporates structural awareness by using Gromov-Monge alignment in quotient spaces, improving sample quality with efficient Gromov-Wasserstein relaxations for tractable training.
AI.motivation: Standard permutation-equivariant architectures don't fully exploit the structural symmetries of graphs. When comparing graph pairs up to node relabeling, the natural geometry is the quotient space, but existing flow matching methods don't properly account for this structural alignment between source and target graphs.
AI.method: Use Gromov-Monge distance (optimal node relabeling) as Euclidean quotient metric for graph pairs. Develop tractable minibatch couplings using efficient Gromov-Wasserstein relaxations for node alignment, optionally combined with outer assignment between graphs. The approach modifies only training couplings while remaining compatible with standard permutation-equivariant architectures.
AI.result: The structure-aware couplings substantially improve sample quality for continuous graph and categorical molecular generation, especially at small integration budgets. Scaled-up molecular models remain competitive under conventional many-step sampling regimes.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating structural alignment through quotient space geometry and Gromov-Monge distances significantly enhances flow matching for graph generation, offering improved sample quality while maintaining compatibility with existing architectures and scaling effectively to larger models.

title: Don't Overthink, Don't Underthink: Toward Adaptive Reasoning in Agentic AI
summary: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown that increased inference-time reasoning can improve performance on complex tasks. However, many existing approaches rely on fixed or preallocated reasoning controls, such as fixed token budgets, pre-execution difficulty estimates, or activation-space interventions, and are often evaluated on standalone reasoning benchmarks rather than full agentic workflows. These assumptions may not hold in agentic AI systems, where reasoning requirements evolve dynamically through planning, tool use, memory retrieval, and agent-to-agent interactions. Consequently, reasoning can become either excessive or insufficient, resulting in unnecessary computation, increased latency, planning drift, excessive tool use, or incomplete solutions. We argue that a major challenge for next-generation agentic AI is not merely how much reasoning a language model should perform, but how it should allocate reasoning according to evolving task demands. We characterize over-reasoning and under-reasoning as recurring failure modes of misallocated reasoning and evaluate them on MATH-500 and the GAIA public validation benchmark. Using tool-decision latency, token consumption, token-limit exhaustion, and answer correctness, our results suggest that cases classified as over-reasoning are associated with higher computational cost without proportional accuracy gains, whereas cases classified as under-reasoning are consistently associated with incorrect or incomplete solutions. These findings motivate future research on adaptive reasoning mechanisms for agentic AI.

AI.tldr: LLMs need adaptive reasoning allocation in agentic AI systems to prevent over-reasoning (excessive computation without accuracy gains) and under-reasoning (incomplete solutions), as current fixed reasoning controls fail to match dynamic task demands.
AI.motivation: Current LLM reasoning approaches use fixed or preallocated controls (fixed token budgets, difficulty estimates) that don't adapt to dynamic agentic workflows involving planning, tool use, memory retrieval, and agent interactions. This leads to misallocated reasoning causing either excessive computation or incomplete solutions.
AI.method: Characterized over-reasoning and under-reasoning as failure modes and evaluated them on MATH-500 and GAIA benchmarks using metrics like tool-decision latency, token consumption, token-limit exhaustion, and answer correctness.
AI.result: Over-reasoning cases showed higher computational cost without proportional accuracy gains, while under-reasoning cases consistently produced incorrect or incomplete solutions. Both failure modes demonstrate the limitations of current fixed reasoning controls.
AI.conclusion: Next-generation agentic AI requires adaptive reasoning mechanisms that allocate reasoning according to evolving task demands rather than fixed controls, as misallocated reasoning in dynamic workflows causes unnecessary computation, latency, planning drift, and incomplete solutions.

title: Packora: Systematic Design for Generative Molecular Crystal Structure Prediction
summary: Molecular crystal structure prediction (CSP) is important in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and organic electronics, where subtle differences in molecular conformation and packing can strongly affect material properties. We present Packora, a flow-based generative model for molecular CSP that jointly predicts atomic coordinates and the lattice from molecular graphs. Packora supports multi-component and organometallic crystals and can condition on any subset of molecular conformers, stereochemical labels, and space-group information within a single model. Inspired by the CCDC CSP blind test, we evaluate generation and ranking separately, using generation to isolate generator quality and ranking to measure end-to-end performance under a common relaxation and ranking pipeline. We also systematically study architecture, training, conditioning, inference, and scaling, identifying an effective design based on cacheable pairwise reasoning, training objective and numerical solver choices, conditioning dropout, and balanced scaling of pairwise and single representations. Packora outperforms the baselines on both structure generation and ranking benchmarks, achieving the best matched-budget coverage across all six generation benchmarks, as well as higher experimental-form recovery, lower experimental-form ranks, and faster convergence in ranking.

AI.tldr: Packora is a flow-based generative model for molecular crystal structure prediction that jointly predicts atomic coordinates and lattice parameters from molecular graphs, supporting multi-component and organometallic crystals with flexible conditioning capabilities.
AI.motivation: Molecular crystal structure prediction (CSP) is crucial in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and organic electronics because subtle differences in molecular conformation and packing can significantly impact material properties. Current methods need improvement in handling diverse crystal types and integrating multiple conditioning information.
AI.method: Packora uses a flow-based generative model architecture that predicts atomic coordinates and lattice jointly from molecular graphs. Key innovations include: 1) cacheable pairwise reasoning, 2) specific training objectives and numerical solver choices, 3) conditioning dropout, and 4) balanced scaling of pairwise and single representations. The method supports multi-component and organometallic crystals with flexible conditioning on molecular conformers, stereochemical labels, and space-group information.
AI.result: Packora outperforms baselines on both structure generation and ranking benchmarks, achieving: 1) best matched-budget coverage across all six generation benchmarks, 2) higher experimental-form recovery rates, 3) lower experimental-form ranks, and 4) faster convergence in ranking tasks. Evaluation follows CCDC CSP blind test methodology with separate generation and ranking assessments.
AI.conclusion: Packora represents an effective flow-based approach to molecular crystal structure prediction that handles diverse crystal types with flexible conditioning, demonstrating superior performance across multiple benchmarks through systematic architecture and training optimizations, making it a promising tool for practical CSP applications in materials science and drug development.

title: PILOT in the Loop: Live Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Long-horizon agent runs generate experience that can improve both the current run and future work. Most self-improvement methods process this experience only after execution ends, so they cannot redirect the active run or immediately apply and validate lessons learned from it. We argue that self-improvement should instead be live, using emerging experience both to redirect the active run and to update the persistent harness. Existing agent architectures do not fully support this goal. Single-agent self-correction combines task execution and trajectory assessment within one context, while subagent delegation separates execution but typically cannot redirect an active subagent. We present PILOT, a supervisor-worker harness for live self-improvement through two coupled mechanisms: (1) live steering lets a separate supervisor redirect or abort the active worker during execution; and (2) live self-evolution distils procedures and failure modes revealed during execution into reusable skills and memory. Across two frozen backbones and three benchmarks, PILOT ranks first in five of six configurations. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, PILOT outperforms counterpart harnesses by up to 9.8 percentage points. In the self-improvement setting, PILOT gains 14.6 points with GLM-5.1 and 12.4 points with Kimi-K2.6. Mean output tokens fall by 42.9% and 47.4%, while successful evaluations per million output tokens rise by 110.3% and 134.0%, respectively.

AI.tldr: PILOT is a supervisor-worker harness that enables live self-improvement in AI agents through real-time steering and skill distillation during execution, significantly improving performance while reducing computational cost.
AI.motivation: Current self-improvement methods process agent experience only after execution ends, preventing real-time redirection and immediate application of lessons learned. Existing architectures either combine execution and assessment in one context (limiting separation) or delegate to subagents without ability to redirect them during execution.
AI.method: PILOT introduces a supervisor-worker harness with two coupled mechanisms: (1) live steering - allows a separate supervisor to redirect or abort the active worker during execution; (2) live self-evolution - distills procedures and failure modes discovered during execution into reusable skills and memory.
AI.result: Across two frozen backbones and three benchmarks, PILOT ranked first in 5 of 6 configurations. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, it outperformed counterpart harnesses by up to 9.8 percentage points. In self-improvement settings, PILOT gained 14.6 points with GLM-5.1 and 12.4 points with Kimi-K2.6, reducing mean output tokens by 42.9-47.4% and increasing successful evaluations per million output tokens by 110.3-134.0%.
AI.conclusion: PILOT successfully demonstrates that live self-improvement through supervisor-worker architecture with real-time steering and skill distillation significantly enhances agent performance and efficiency compared to post-hoc self-improvement approaches.

title: Adversarial Training Without Input Gradients via Low-Rank Householder Expansions
summary: This work concerns adversarial training against the small-norm adversarial examples that arise from the inherent input instability of a trained deep neural network. Examples in this class are small as measured in the relative $\ell^2$-norm, and therefore lie in the neighborhood of the input on which the model acts approximately linearly, the regime in which the perturbation remains imperceptible. We first show that such examples can be computed directly from the trained network parameters, without input gradient iterations, by means of a linearization called the low-rank Householder expansion (LRHE). The expansion describes the composed affine map rather than any individual layer, and the directions it identifies are read from the activation pattern already available in the forward pass. We then propose a simple adversarial training scheme built on this construction. No differentiation with respect to the input is performed at any point: training requires only additional forward evaluations, with weight parameters updated by the standard backward pass, and the inner maximization of the usual min-max formulation is eliminated entirely. That such a regularizer exists is our main finding: the methods that dispense with the inner search all obtain their local geometry by differentiating with respect to the input, and we show this is not necessary. The regularizer costs the equivalent of $2.8$ PGD steps per epoch, an $8.7\times$ reduction relative to 40-step adversarial training on MNIST and below the cost of 3-step training. The resulting models match three-step PGD adversarial training for relative $\ell^2$ budgets $\varepsilon \le 0.02$ and 40-step training for $\varepsilon \le 0.012$, falling away beyond, consistent with the locality of the expansion.

AI.tldr: Adversarial training without gradient-based inner maximization using linearized perturbations from network parameters.
AI.motivation: Current adversarial training methods require expensive gradient computations and inner maximization loops to defend against small-norm adversarial examples. The authors aim to develop a more efficient method that avoids input differentiation while still protecting against small perturbations in the approximately linear region around inputs.
AI.method: The authors use a low-rank Householder expansion (LRHE) to compute adversarial examples directly from trained network parameters without input gradient iterations. This expansion captures the composed affine map of the network using activation patterns from the forward pass. They propose an adversarial training scheme that eliminates inner maximization entirely - training requires only additional forward evaluations with standard backward weight updates.
AI.result: The method achieves 8.7× reduction in computational cost compared to 40-step PGD adversarial training, costing only the equivalent of 2.8 PGD steps per epoch. The resulting models match or exceed standard adversarial training performance for small perturbation budgets (ε ≤ 0.02 for 3-step PGD, ε ≤ 0.012 for 40-step PGD), but performance degrades for larger perturbations beyond this linear regime.
AI.conclusion: The main finding is that adversarial regularization can be achieved without input differentiation or inner maximization loops. The LRHE-based method provides efficient protection against small-norm adversarial examples in the approximately linear region around inputs, demonstrating that local adversarial geometry can be obtained directly from network parameters rather than through gradient-based search.

title: Multi2AV-Safety: Benchmarking Safety in Multimodal-to-Audio-Video Generation
summary: Audio-video generation is rapidly moving from prompt-driven synthesis toward multimodal conditioning, where text, images, audio, and video can jointly shape the generated output. This shift changes the nature of safety evaluation: harmful intent may no longer reside in any single input, but instead emerge from how otherwise benign or weakly harmful conditions interact across modalities and time. Existing safety benchmarks, however, remain largely prompt-centric or tied to fixed conditioning interfaces, leaving such compositional risks difficult to study systematically. To bridge this gap, we introduce Multi2AV-Safety, the first safety benchmark, to the best of our knowledge, to cover all 11 non-singleton T/I/A/V conditioning configurations for audio-video generation, comprising 11,024 attack instances. Evaluation on Multi2AV-Safety reveals systematic weaknesses in representative multimodal safety guards across attack mechanisms and harm-evidence structures. Our evaluation reveals two complementary failure modes: harmful semantics can emerge from the combination of individually benign inputs, while explicit harmful cues can become harder to detect when mixed with benign multimodal context. Together, these results identify \emph{compositional risk perception} as a central capability gap in safeguarding multimodal-conditioned audio-video generation: current safety guards fail to reliably integrate safety evidence across modalities and time, even when all conditioning inputs are observable. The dataset will be publicly released in October 2026.

AI.tldr: Multi2AV-Safety: First safety benchmark covering all 11 multimodal conditioning configurations for audio-video generation, revealing systematic weaknesses in current safety guards against compositional risks where harmful intent emerges from interactions across modalities and time.
AI.motivation: Audio-video generation is shifting from prompt-driven synthesis to multimodal conditioning (text, images, audio, video). This creates new safety challenges where harmful intent can emerge from interactions between otherwise benign inputs across modalities and time, rather than from single harmful prompts. Existing safety benchmarks are prompt-centric and can't systematically evaluate these compositional risks.
AI.method: Developed Multi2AV-Safety benchmark covering all 11 non-singleton text/image/audio/video conditioning configurations for audio-video generation (11,024 attack instances). Evaluated representative multimodal safety guards across various attack mechanisms and harm-evidence structures to systematically assess compositional risks.
AI.result: Revealed systematic weaknesses in current multimodal safety guards. Identified two complementary failure modes: 1) Harmful semantics emerging from combinations of individually benign inputs, 2) Explicit harmful cues becoming harder to detect when mixed with benign multimodal context. Current guards fail to integrate safety evidence across modalities and time effectively.
AI.conclusion: Compositional risk perception is a central capability gap in safeguarding multimodal-conditioned audio-video generation. Current safety approaches fail to reliably handle safety evidence integration across modalities and time, even with observable inputs. The benchmark enables systematic study of these emerging risks, with dataset release planned for October 2026.

title: Graph-Based Pseudo-multimodal Contrastive Learning for 12-Lead ECG Representations
comment: 7 pages, 7 figures. Presented at the 48th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC 2026)
summary:
12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is a standard, non-invasive examination widely used for diagnosing coronary artery disease, where clinical interpretation relies on comparing waveform patterns across multiple leads. However, most existing ECG analysis methods focus on single-lead signals or treat each lead independently, and typically process ECG signals as one-dimensional time-series data using CNNs or RNNs. While effective in modeling local waveform changes, such approaches have difficulty capturing inter-lead dependency and global waveform patterns essential for clinical diagnosis.
  To address this limitation, we propose a graph-based pseudo-multimodal contrastive learning framework called Graph-CMMC. ECG waveforms are transformed into Gramian Angular Difference Field (GADF) images to construct complementary representations of the same cardiac activity, enabling a pseudo-multimodal learning setting. Using all 12 leads, Graph-CMMC aligns waveform and GADF representations in a self-supervised manner, while a graph-based relational module is employed to model inter-lead dependency and enforce structural consistency across leads during contrastive learning.
  Experimental results on a multi-label coronary artery occlusion classification task demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance compared to supervised learning methods. These results further suggest the effectiveness of using GADF as a complementary representation and incorporating explicit graph-based modeling of inter-lead dependency for learning robust 12-lead ECG representations.

AI.tldr: Proposes Graph-CMMC: a graph-based pseudo-multimodal contrastive learning framework for 12-lead ECG analysis that uses GADF images as complementary representations and models inter-lead dependencies with graph structure.
AI.motivation: Current ECG analysis methods typically focus on single-lead signals or treat leads independently, processing ECGs as 1D time-series with CNNs/RNNs.
