These approaches fail to capture inter-lead dependencies and global waveform patterns that are clinically essential for diagnosing coronary artery disease.
AI.method: Transforms ECG waveforms into Gramian Angular Difference Field (GADF) images to create complementary representations. Uses all 12 leads in a self-supervised contrastive learning framework that aligns waveform and GADF representations. Incorporates a graph-based relational module to model inter-lead dependencies and enforce structural consistency across leads during contrastive learning.
AI.result: The framework achieves competitive performance on multi-label coronary artery occlusion classification tasks compared to supervised learning methods. Results show effectiveness of using GADF as complementary representation and graph-based modeling of inter-lead dependencies for learning robust 12-lead ECG representations.
AI.conclusion: Graph-CMMC effectively addresses limitations of traditional ECG analysis by capturing inter-lead dependencies and global patterns. The graph-based pseudo-multimodal contrastive learning approach with GADF representations enables robust ECG feature learning for clinical applications like coronary artery disease diagnosis.

title: DuMateBench: Evaluating Autonomous Agents in Complex Real-World Workflows
summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly adopted to complete complex, multi-tool workflows in real-world settings. However, existing benchmarks typically separate tasks by application or capability and evaluate agents in environments that are cleaner and more stable than those encountered in practice. We introduce DuMateBench, a real-session benchmark reconstructed from anonymized and privacy-screened user sessions collected from a large-scale production agent platform. Each task preserves the relevant pre-solution interaction history, persistent configurations, and workspace state, and is then validated through human verification. The resulting benchmark comprises 200 tasks spanning 8 broad scenarios and 17 fine-grained capability categories, with most tasks requiring multiple capability coordination. We execute these tasks in isolated Docker containers injected with three forms of real-world environmental complexity: Insufficient, Unstable, and Noisy, and assess performance using a hybrid deterministic and LLM-as-Judge evaluation protocol. Experiments across five representative autonomous-agent frameworks paired with four state-of-the-art LLMs reveal substantial gaps in strict task completion. Complementary robustness, efficiency, and diagnostic analyses further show that performance under environmental perturbations is jointly shaped by the capabilities of the LLM and the surrounding agent framework. The code and data are publicly available at https://dumatebench.com/.

AI.tldr: DuMateBench is a real-world benchmark for autonomous agents using anonymized user sessions from production platforms, featuring 200 multi-step tasks with environmental complexities (Insufficient, Unstable, Noisy), revealing substantial performance gaps in current agent frameworks.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate agents in clean, stable environments and separate tasks by application/capability, failing to capture the complex, messy real-world conditions agents face in production settings.
AI.method: Created benchmark from anonymized user sessions from production agent platform, preserving interaction history, configurations, and workspace state. Tasks executed in isolated Docker containers with three environmental complexities: Insufficient, Unstable, and Noisy. Evaluated using hybrid deterministic and LLM-as-Judge protocol across 5 agent frameworks and 4 state-of-the-art LLMs.
AI.result: Substantial gaps in strict task completion were found. Performance under environmental perturbations is jointly shaped by LLM capabilities and agent framework design, with complementary robustness, efficiency, and diagnostic analyses supporting these findings.
AI.conclusion: DuMateBench provides a realistic evaluation platform that reveals critical performance limitations in current autonomous agents when faced with real-world complexities, highlighting the need for more robust agent frameworks that can handle production environmental challenges.

title: ClusterAttention: A training-free speedup of bidirectional attention
summary:
This paper introduces ClusterAttention, a general training-free speedup of bidirectional attention layers. Existing sparse attention methods either rely on structure in the input, such as order in language or spatial proximity in images, or use slow clustering processes amortized over several forward passes. ClusterAttention instead uses a fast recursive clustering method that adapts to the geometry of the keys and queries in each attention head to produce useful clusters. This method allows setting the size of the clusters arbitrarily. We utilize this by setting all clusters to be a fixed size that is a power of two, allowing the block-sparse attention to run at the same latency per query-key interaction as dense attention on GPUs. We also derive an expression for the output error in sparse attention, that explains the counterintuitive experimental finding that tight clusters can lead to larger errors than random clusters. We then derive the error when excluded clusters are compensated through their centroids, and show that this error shrinks with tighter clusters. We integrate this compensation into the method.
  On large-scale tabular data ClusterAttention speeds up TabPFN-3 arXiv:2605.13986 by two to six times, while retaining at least 99% of the dense accuracy. To our knowledge, it is the first training-free method that can be successfully applied in the setting of unstructured input and a single forward pass. For video generation with Wan 2.1-14B T2V arXiv:2503.20314 , ClusterAttention achieves output closer to dense attention and a larger speedup (1.8x versus 1.4x) compared to SVOO arXiv:2603.18636 , a leading method developed specifically for this domain, both run without offline calibration.

AI.tldr: ClusterAttention is a training-free method that speeds up bidirectional attention layers using fast recursive clustering that adapts to key-query geometry, allowing arbitrary cluster sizes while maintaining GPU efficiency through power-of-two sizing.
AI.motivation: Existing sparse attention methods either rely on input structure (language order, spatial proximity) or use slow clustering processes amortized over multiple forward passes, limiting their applicability to unstructured inputs and single-forward-pass scenarios.
AI.method: Uses fast recursive clustering that adapts to key-query geometry in each attention head, allows arbitrary cluster sizing with power-of-two clusters for GPU efficiency, derives error expressions for sparse attention, and includes compensation for excluded clusters via centroids.
AI.result: Achieves 2-6x speedup on TabPFN-3 with ≥99% dense accuracy, 1.8x speedup on Wan 2.1-14B T2V video generation (better than SVOO's 1.4x), and is the first training-free method successful for unstructured inputs with single forward pass.
AI.conclusion: ClusterAttention provides an effective training-free speedup for attention layers that works across diverse domains (tabular data, video generation), adapts to input geometry, maintains accuracy, and outperforms domain-specific methods while being generally applicable.

title: AgentJudgeBench: A Multi-Difficulty Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Judges on Agentic Tool-Calling
comment: 31 Pages, 9 Figures, 31 Tables, Accepted as a main conference paper at EMNLP 2026
summary: LLM judges are widely used to evaluate agentic tool-calling systems, yet their reliability on structured, dependency-driven workflows remains largely unexamined. We present AgentJudgeBench, the first benchmark to systematically study LLM-as-a-judge reliability for agentic tool-calling over workflow DAGs, as distinct from the broader LLM-as-a-judge task of open-ended text or preference evaluation. The benchmark comprises 3,808 instances spanning six DAG topologies and three difficulty tiers, evaluated with five generators (3B-70B open-weight models and GPT-5.4) and six judges (20B to frontier scale) under paired with- and without-ground-truth conditions. Judge alignment degrades monotonically with task difficulty, 1.5x faster without ground truth, and on hard queries without ground truth all six judges converge to a narrow 77-82% band regardless of scale, revealing a structural ceiling driven primarily by task difficulty, though its height is partly prompt-dependent for weaker generators, that model capacity alone cannot overcome. Ground-truth exposure is not uniformly beneficial: it reduces alignment for GPT-5.4 (1.5 pp) and Gemini-2.5-Pro (3.9 pp), consistent with over-anchoring. Among mitigation strategies, chain-of-thought reasoning and judge temperature both have negligible effect, while structured evaluation rubrics improve alignment by up to 6.5 pp but do not generalize uniformly across judge-generator pairs. With ground truth, QwQ-32B best matches the programmatic reference, while a human validation study identifies GPT-OSS-120B as the most human-aligned judge; without it, frontier judges lead only marginally within the shared ceiling. These results expose fundamental limitations of current LLM judges and yield practical guidelines for reliable evaluation in agentic systems.

AI.tldr: LLM judges are unreliable for evaluating complex agentic tool-calling workflows, especially without ground truth, with performance limited by task difficulty rather than model scale.
AI.motivation: Current LLM judges are widely used to evaluate agentic tool-calling systems, but their reliability on structured, dependency-driven workflows remains largely unexamined.
AI.method: Created AgentJudgeBench with 3,808 instances across six DAG topologies and three difficulty tiers, evaluating five generators (3B-70B models) and six judges (20B to frontier scale) with/without ground truth, plus human validation study.
AI.result: Judge alignment degrades with task difficulty, converging to 77-82% band on hard queries without ground truth regardless of model scale; ground truth can reduce alignment for some models; structured rubrics help but don't generalize well; QwQ-32B best with ground truth, GPT-OSS-120B most human-aligned.
AI.conclusion: Reveals fundamental limitations of current LLM judges for agentic workflows, showing performance is constrained by task difficulty rather than model capacity, providing practical guidelines for reliable evaluation.

title: TEMPLAR Wales: A georeferenced environmental and toponymic dataset of Welsh settlements
summary: Place names provide persistent records of how landscapes have been described and organised, but their quantitative reuse requires explicit separation between mapped places, lexical annotations and environmental measurements. TEMPLAR Wales is a georeferenced environmental-toponymy dataset comprising 3,757 settlement records across Wales. The resource links a reproducible settlement frame to deterministic lexical screening and settlement-level environmental attributes through stable identifiers. It contains 1,350 lexical detections across 1,294 settlements, generated from a frozen registry of 24 Welsh place-name elements, while retaining exact- and prefix-token matches and their provenance separately. Environmental attributes describe river and coastal proximity, elevation and local terrain context at multiple spatial scales, land cover and neighbourhood woody cover, with parallel terrain measurements derived from independent elevation products. The dataset is distributed as four relational tables accompanied by a field-level data dictionary, source-provenance register and licensing metadata. Technical validation confirms relational integrity, deterministic lexical reconstruction, documented environmental coverage, strong agreement between independent terrain sources and reproducible reconstruction of the frozen release. TEMPLAR Wales provides a reusable foundation for research in toponymy, linguistic geography, historical and environmental landscape studies, GIS and spatial data analysis without treating computational lexical detections as verified etymologies or contemporary environmental measurements as historical landscape reconstructions.

AI.tldr: A georeferenced dataset linking Welsh place names with environmental attributes and lexical annotations for quantitative research in toponymy and landscape studies.
AI.motivation: Place names offer valuable historical records of landscape organization, but their quantitative analysis requires systematic separation of mapped locations, lexical elements, and environmental measurements for reliable research.
AI.method: Created TEMPLAR Wales dataset with 3,757 settlement records linking reproducible settlement framework to deterministic lexical screening using 24 Welsh place-name elements, generating 1,350 lexical detections across 1,294 settlements. Environmental attributes include river/coastal proximity, elevation, terrain context at multiple scales, land cover, and woody cover, with parallel terrain measurements from independent elevation products.
AI.result: Produced a validated dataset with four relational tables, data dictionary, provenance register, and licensing metadata. Technical validation confirmed relational integrity, deterministic lexical reconstruction, documented environmental coverage, strong agreement between terrain sources, and reproducible reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: TEMPLAR Wales provides a reusable foundation for interdisciplinary research in toponymy, linguistic geography, historical/environmental landscape studies, and spatial analysis, while maintaining clear distinctions between computational detections and verified etymologies, and between current environmental measurements and historical reconstructions.

title: Terrain signatures in Welsh settlement names
summary: Landscapes are named, but whether names retain measurable environmental information beyond broad geographic structure is rarely tested. We analysed 3,757 Welsh settlements using a frozen, source-audited 24-element lexical framework, preregistered outcome-specific models and geographically structured validation. The central comparison contrasted 101 settlements carrying high-terrain elements (\textit{bryn} or \textit{mynydd}) with 139 carrying low-terrain elements (\textit{cwm} or \textit{pant}). High-terrain names occupied locations 24.4 m higher relative to their 2-km surroundings (95\% CI, 10.8--38.1 m; Holm-adjusted $p$ = 0.00137). The association remained positive across prespecified 1-, 2- and 5-km neighbourhood definitions and was reproduced using an independently produced elevation source (24.1 m; 95\% CI, 10.6--37.6 m). Adding terrain-name polarity to a non-lexical spatial and settlement baseline reduced geographically held-out mean squared error by 4.63\%, 6.22\% and 7.30\% under 10-, 25- and 50-km spatial blocking, respectively, although improvement varied among held-out regions. River-related names provided weaker, directionally consistent evidence, while the preregistered woodland model was non-estimable. Residual spatial structure, unresolved name language and the absence of independent external replication limit interpretation. Selected Welsh settlement-name categories therefore retain measurable information about present-day terrain within Wales, without establishing individual etymology, causal naming, historical environmental memory or transferability to other naming systems.

AI.tldr: Welsh settlement names containing high-terrain words (bryn/mynydd) vs. low-terrain words (cwm/pant) accurately predict actual terrain elevation differences - high-terrain names occur 24m higher than low-terrain names, showing place names retain measurable environmental information.
AI.motivation: To test whether landscape names retain measurable environmental information beyond broad geographic patterns, specifically examining Welsh settlement names for terrain-related elements.
AI.method: Analyzed 3,757 Welsh settlements using a frozen 24-element lexical framework with preregistered outcome-specific models. Used geographically structured validation with spatial blocking (10-, 25-, 50-km). Main comparison: 101 settlements with high-terrain elements (bryn/mynydd) vs. 139 with low-terrain elements (cwm/pant) across multiple neighborhood definitions.
AI.result: High-terrain names occupied locations 24.4m higher relative to 2-km surroundings (95% CI: 10.8-38.1m, p=0.00137). Association persisted across 1-, 2-, 5-km neighborhoods and independent elevation data. Adding terrain-name polarity reduced geographically held-out mean squared error by 4.63-7.30%. River-related names showed weaker evidence; woodland model was non-estimable.
AI.conclusion: Selected Welsh settlement-name categories retain measurable information about present-day terrain within Wales, but findings don't establish individual etymology, causal naming, historical environmental memory, or transferability to other naming systems.

title: Relational Over-Regularization: Graph-Based AI-Generated Text Detection via Sentence Transition Deviation
summary: Detecting AI-generated text (AIGT) remains challenging because existing approaches rely on token-level statistical signals or independent stylometric features, causing them to overfit to specific generators and fail under distribution shift. We identify a structural signal at the sentence-pair level: LLMs produce inter-sentence transition variance that deviates from human writing through inflated variance driven by recurring similarity bursts at paragraph boundaries and templated transitions. We formalize this as Relational Over-Regularization (ROR) and validate it across four benchmarks (p < 0.001). The central contribution is this relational problem formulation, not a novel GNN architecture; CSFG is one concrete instantiation for operationalizing ROR. To exploit this signal, we propose the Cross-Source Stylometric Fingerprint Graph (CSFG), a graph-based framework that encodes positional, sequential, semantic, and transition deviation signals as learnable GNN edge features. The per-edge signed deviation δ_ij operationalizes ROR without hand-crafted thresholds and acts as a false-positive calibrator. CSFG achieves 97.14% accuracy under binary detection, outperforming the strongest graph-based baseline by 11.14 pp, with a false-positive rate of 1.57% and robust generalization to unseen LLMs in the inflated-variance regime; detection degrades for generators whose transition variance falls at or below the human baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CSFG, a graph-based framework that detects AI-generated text by identifying inflated inter-sentence transition variance (Relational Over-Regularization) as a key structural signal that distinguishes LLM output from human writing.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-generated text detection methods rely on token-level statistical signals or independent stylometric features, causing them to overfit to specific generators and fail under distribution shift. There's a need for more robust detection approaches that can generalize to unseen LLMs.
AI.method: The paper identifies Relational Over-Regularization (ROR) - a structural signal at the sentence-pair level where LLMs produce inter-sentence transition variance that deviates from human writing through recurring similarity bursts at paragraph boundaries and templated transitions. The Cross-Source Stylometric Fingerprint Graph (CSFG) framework encodes positional, sequential, semantic, and transition deviation signals as learnable GNN edge features, with per-edge signed deviation δ_ij operationalizing ROR without hand-crafted thresholds.
AI.result: CSFG achieves 97.14% accuracy under binary detection, outperforming the strongest graph-based baseline by 11.14 percentage points, with a false-positive rate of 1.57% and robust generalization to unseen LLMs in the inflated-variance regime. Detection degrades for generators whose transition variance falls at or below the human baseline.
AI.conclusion: The key contribution is the relational problem formulation (ROR) rather than a novel GNN architecture, with CSFG being one concrete instantiation for operationalizing this insight. The approach successfully exploits structural differences in inter-sentence transitions to create a more robust AI-generated text detection system.

title: Decentralized Multitask Learning over Learned Task Graphs
summary: This paper investigates decentralized multitask learning over networks when the underlying task relationships are unknown. While existing graph-regularized multitask frameworks typically assume a known structure, practical settings often require learning inter-task dependencies directly from distributed data. We propose a decentralized two-phase strategy that first estimates a generalized graph Laplacian from noisy non-cooperative stochastic gradient iterates, and subsequently exploits the learned graph to enable cooperative multitask diffusion learning. This framework is motivated by a Gaussian Markov random field prior, which gives rise to a decentralized maximum likelihood estimator for the graph Laplacian. The analysis quantifies the Laplacian estimation error and its propagation to the steady-state performance of the multitask diffusion recursion, and introduces a topology sensitivity index to capture the effect of network heterogeneity. Simulation results corroborate the theoretical findings and demonstrate that cooperation enabled by the learned task graph significantly improves performance over non-cooperative learning, while approaching the true-graph baseline when the estimation stepsize is sufficiently small.

AI.tldr: Decentralized multitask learning with unknown task relationships: learn graph structure from data first, then use it for cooperative learning, achieving near-optimal performance with small stepsize.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-regularized multitask learning methods assume known task relationships, but in practical decentralized settings over networks, the underlying task dependencies are often unknown and need to be learned directly from distributed data.
AI.method: Two-phase decentralized strategy: 1) estimate generalized graph Laplacian from noisy non-cooperative stochastic gradient iterates using maximum likelihood estimator derived from Gaussian Markov random field prior, 2) use learned graph for cooperative multitask diffusion learning.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis quantifies Laplacian estimation error and its propagation to steady-state performance, introduces topology sensitivity index for network heterogeneity effects. Simulations show learned graph cooperation significantly outperforms non-cooperative learning and approaches true-graph baseline with sufficiently small estimation stepsize.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables effective decentralized multitask learning when task relationships are unknown, with learned cooperation providing substantial performance gains over non-cooperative approaches and approaching optimal performance when estimation parameters are properly tuned.

title: Five Primitives for Governing Autonomous AI Agents at Runtime
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Describes an implemented system in private pilot deployment; four of five primitives implemented
summary: Enterprise deployments of autonomous AI agents inherit a control model built for human users and long-lived services, and the fit fails in three specific ways: agent principals are ephemeral, appearing and vanishing faster than provisioning; their actions are selected by a model rather than programmed, so the set of things they may attempt is not known in advance; and the population is discovered rather than provisioned, because anyone who can call an API can create one. We argue that governing such agents is a runtime problem -- not a model-alignment problem and not a build-time problem -- and we derive five primitives from the questions that must be answered before an action takes effect and after it has: discovery, identity, governance, attestation, and supply chain. For each we state what fails if it is absent and why the others cannot structurally supply it. We describe an implementation in which an agent's action is mediated against policy before it takes effect, authorised against a per-tenant action vocabulary, and recorded in a hash-linked signed ledger a third party can verify with the vendor out of the loop. We report what the architecture costs: the enforcement point sits on the request's critical path, identity requires a sidecar per workload, and fail-closed mediation converts availability incidents into denial. We are explicit about implementation status: four primitives are built and running in private pilots, and the fifth is built as separate tooling and not yet integrated into the request path. We keep it in the set deliberately: a five-part decomposition that exactly matches what its authors happened to build is not a taxonomy but a description of a codebase.

AI.tldr: AI agents require runtime governance with five primitives (discovery, identity, governance, attestation, supply chain) because they differ fundamentally from traditional human users and services in their ephemerality, unpredictable actions, and spontaneous creation.
AI.motivation: Current enterprise control models fail for autonomous AI agents because: 1) agents are ephemeral (appear/vanish faster than provisioning), 2) their actions are model-selected rather than programmed (unpredictable action sets), and 3) they're discovered rather than provisioned (anyone can create via API). Traditional human-user and service-oriented governance approaches don't fit.
AI.method: Propose runtime governance with five primitives: discovery (detecting agents), identity (establishing agent identity), governance (policy mediation before actions), attestation (verifying past actions), and supply chain (verifying agent components). Implement a system where agent actions are mediated against policy, authorized against per-tenant vocabularies, and recorded in a hash-linked signed ledger for third-party verification.
AI.result: Implementation shows trade-offs: enforcement sits on critical path, identity requires sidecar per workload, fail-closed mediation converts availability incidents into denial. Four primitives are built and running in private pilots; fifth (supply chain) is built as separate tooling but not yet integrated into request path.
AI.conclusion: Governing AI agents is a runtime problem requiring specific primitives, not a model-alignment or build-time issue. The proposed five-part decomposition provides a structured approach, though implementation reveals practical costs. The authors deliberately keep all five primitives to avoid presenting just a description of their codebase.

title: Benchmarking_Fast_Domain_Adaptation_for_Unsupervised_Speech_Units
summary: Representation learning has attracted great atten- tion and managed to reach good performances as a pretraining method for downstream tasks or as a first step towards unsu- pervised speech modeling. Yet, little is known about how such methods deal with out-of-domain speech and how could they be adapted in a few shot to new domains. This is important especially for accented speech where one observes a long tail of accents that diverge from the standard ones. We introduce ABX- Accent, a benchmark based on the AESRC dataset that features 10 different accents of English. It includes a small (< 10 hours) unlabelled training set in each of the accents and adaptations of the Zero Resources Challenge ABX evaluation metrics to each of the accents. We illustrate this benchmark with a baseline model that uses adaptive domain normalization to fine tune a pretrained Contrastive Predictive Coding model on the accents. This method is first developed on LibriSpeech using a male/female split. When applied to the new benchmark, the proposed method yields a relative improvement of 23.6% on across-speaker ABX scores on average compared to non adapted models. The data and metrics will be open sourced upon paper acceptance

AI.tldr: ABX-Accent benchmark evaluates representation learning models on accented speech adaptation, showing 23.6% improvement with adaptive domain normalization.
AI.motivation: Limited understanding of how representation learning methods handle out-of-domain speech, particularly important for accented speech where there's a long tail of accents diverging from standard ones. Need to evaluate adaptation to new domains with few-shot learning.
AI.method: Introduces ABX-Accent benchmark based on AESRC dataset with 10 English accents, each with small (<10 hours) unlabelled training sets. Uses adaptive domain normalization to fine-tune pretrained Contrastive Predictive Coding models on accents, first developed on LibriSpeech with male/female split.
AI.result: Proposed adaptive domain normalization method achieves 23.6% relative improvement on average across-speaker ABX scores compared to non-adapted models when applied to the new benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The ABX-Accent benchmark enables evaluation of representation learning on accented speech adaptation, demonstrating significant improvements with adaptive domain normalization for few-shot adaptation to new accents.

title: Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini in the Real-World
summary: We present an extension and comprehensive real-world validation of Co-Scientist, a Gemini-based multi-agent system designed to accelerate end-to-end scientific research across hypothesis generation, experimentation, and manuscript generation. Moving beyond in silico hypothesis generation, this specialized configuration transitions Co-Scientist into an execution-grounded research partner advancing closed-loop scientific workflows across materials science, biology, and computer science. In materials science, Co-Scientist interfaced with a semi-automated chemical vapor deposition reactor to design a safe precursor route for MXenes; experimental execution produced a lamellar 2D material sharing key structural similarities with the Ti3C2Tx MXene lattice, although further experiments are needed to confirm the atomic structure. Leveraging Gemini 3 Deep Think for rapid, lab-in-the-loop execution, it also tailored growth recipes to laboratory constraints in minutes, enabling single-attempt growth of monolayer MoS2, MoSe2, and WS2 semiconductors. In biology, Co-Scientist predicted emergent swarming phenotypes of engineered E. coli across inducer (IPTG) gradients from sparse imaging data, quantitatively matching unpublished wet-lab morphological measurements. In computer science, Co-Scientist autonomously discovered an inference-time scaling architecture that outperformed six frontier models on HealthBench (Hard and Professional) while reducing potential clinical harm under blinded physician evaluation. Finally, a double-blind study of end-to-end generated papers with 30 domain experts across 450 reviews demonstrates that Co-Scientist's reliability modules reduce hallucination and plagiarism while improving research safety. Together, these results demonstrate progress toward closed-loop multi-agent scientific AI systems capable of accelerating real-world scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: Co-Scientist, a Gemini-based multi-agent AI system, accelerates end-to-end scientific research through automated hypothesis generation, experimental execution, and manuscript writing, validated across materials science, biology, and computer science.
AI.motivation: To advance beyond in silico hypothesis generation and create an execution-grounded research partner that can accelerate real-world scientific discovery across multiple disciplines through closed-loop workflows.
AI.method: Extension of Co-Scientist using Gemini-based multi-agent system with specialized configurations for different scientific domains. System interfaces with laboratory equipment (chemical vapor deposition reactor), uses Gemini 3 Deep Think for rapid lab-in-the-loop execution, processes sparse imaging data for biological predictions, and employs reliability modules to reduce AI hallucinations and plagiarism.
AI.result: In materials science: designed safe precursor route for MXenes producing lamellar 2D material; achieved single-attempt growth of monolayer MoS2, MoSe2, and WS2 semiconductors. In biology: accurately predicted emergent swarming phenotypes of engineered E. coli matching unpublished wet-lab measurements. In computer science: autonomously discovered inference-time scaling architecture outperforming six frontier models on HealthBench while reducing clinical harm. Double-blind study with 30 domain experts across 450 reviews showed reduced hallucination and plagiarism.
AI.conclusion: Co-Scientist demonstrates significant progress toward closed-loop multi-agent scientific AI systems capable of accelerating real-world scientific discovery across multiple domains, moving from hypothesis generation to actual experimental execution and manuscript generation with improved reliability and safety.

title: Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO
summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a widely used objective for aligning language models from preference data, with the coefficient $β$ commonly interpreted as controlling the KL constraint to a reference policy. We show that $β$ entangles two distinct roles: it governs the effective inverse preference-noise scale and simultaneously rescales the optimization dynamics, coupling this scale with the effective step size. As a consequence, at a fixed learning rate the achieved policy deviation is non-monotone in $β$: it vanishes in a dead zone at small $β$, reaches a peak at an intermediate value, and decreases again for larger $β$. Moreover, standard DPO loss values are not comparable across $β$: runs with nearly identical loss curves can differ several-fold in KL divergence from the reference model. This entanglement obscures the role of $β$, increases sensitivity to hyperparameter choices, and complicates learning-rate scheduling. We propose a centered-softplus reformulation that is argmin-equivalent to DPO for $β>0$, while making the inverse preference-noise-scale and learning-rate effects explicit and independently tunable. The normalized centered-softplus objective also admits a continuous $β\to0$ endpoint that reduces to a linear preference-margin objective.

AI.tldr: DPO's β coefficient is problematic because it conflates preference-noise scale with optimization dynamics, causing non-monotonic policy changes and making loss values incomparable across β values.
AI.motivation: The paper identifies that Direct Preference Optimization's β parameter, commonly interpreted as controlling KL constraint, actually entangles two distinct roles: it governs inverse preference-noise scale and rescales optimization dynamics simultaneously, causing issues with interpretation and optimization.
AI.method: Proposes a centered-softplus reformulation that is argmin-equivalent to DPO for β>0, making inverse preference-noise-scale and learning-rate effects explicit and independently tunable. The normalized version also admits a continuous β→0 endpoint reducing to a linear preference-margin objective.
AI.result: Shows that standard DPO has problematic behavior: policy deviation is non-monotone in β (vanishes at small β, peaks at intermediate values, decreases at large β), and loss values are not comparable across β values.
AI.conclusion: The entanglement in DPO's β parameter obscures its role, increases sensitivity to hyperparameters, and complicates learning-rate scheduling. The proposed centered-softplus formulation resolves these issues by making the effects explicit and independently tunable.

title: Style as a Confound: False Positives in AI Detection of Non-Native Academic Writing
summary: AI text detectors are increasingly employed in academic settings, but it remains unclear whether their outputs reflect AI authorship itself or broader linguistic features associated with polished academic English. Previous studies have reported high false-positive rates (FPRs) for non-native English writing, but population-level comparisons confound authorship with differences in topic, domain, and writing style. Professional editing provides a useful setting for examining this issue because it changes the linguistic form of manuscripts while preserving authorship and content. We examined 135,389 document pairs from a professional English editing service (2018-2025), comprising non-native manuscripts and their native-edited versions, to assess how editing affects detector responses controlling for content and authorship. For the 13 AI text detectors, FPRs for human-written texts varied widely, from 0.0% to 100.0%. Responses varied across detectors: the same edits increased AI scores in some detectors but decreased them in others. Notably, score changes correlated with the extent of editing. The findings identify professional editing style as a key confounding variable in AI detector outputs, rather than establishing a full separation of text origin from linguistic style, raising concerns about fairness and reliability in academic settings.

AI.tldr: AI text detectors show high false-positive rates for professionally edited human-written manuscripts, with editing style confounding detector outputs rather than true AI authorship detection.
AI.motivation: There is uncertainty whether AI text detectors identify AI authorship or simply respond to polished academic English features, especially given high false-positive rates for non-native English writing in previous studies.
AI.method: Analyzed 135,389 document pairs from a professional English editing service (2018-2025) comprising non-native manuscripts and their native-edited versions, testing 13 AI text detectors to assess how editing affects detector responses while controlling for content and authorship.
AI.result: False-positive rates varied widely (0.0%-100.0%) across detectors; editing caused inconsistent score changes (increased in some detectors, decreased in others); score changes correlated with editing extent; professional editing style emerged as a key confounding variable.
AI.conclusion: AI detector outputs are confounded by professional editing style rather than establishing clear separation between AI-generated and human-written text, raising significant fairness and reliability concerns in academic settings.

title: Performance Foundations of Parallel & Distributed Reasoning Language Models
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) and other RL-style post-training paradigms have been used for aligning large language models (LLMs) with reasoning standards. The resulting recent Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) such as DeepSeek-R1, o3, and Kimi k1.5 show that such RL-style post-training ("RL-for-LLMs") can substantially improve chain-of-thought reasoning, long-horizon planning, and self-correction. However, the computational footprint of these systems is massive: state-of-the-art RLM training requires millions of GPU-hours and tightly coupled multi-model pipelines that stress modern hardware far beyond classical supervised LLM training. This makes RLM training as much a parallel and distributed systems problem as an algorithmic one. In this work, to facilitate developing RLMs that are simultaneously high-performance, scalable, and cost-effective, we first systematize the RL-for-LLM paradigm and provide a compute-centric analysis of prominent post-training algorithmic frameworks: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), as well as their variants. Second, we develop a taxonomy of intra- and inter-model parallelism strategies for RL-for-LLMs, covering both traditional techniques (data, tensor, pipeline, sequence, context, and expert parallelism) as well as novel forms of parallelism and optimization techniques for multi-model RLM training, for example disaggregated placement, stage fusion, hybrid parallelism, and asynchronous execution. We harness the work-depth model of parallel computing to make our taxonomy and its insights rigorous and portable. Finally, we analyze existing RLM frameworks and we distill practical guidelines and outline open research directions for building scalable, fast, and cost-effective RLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper systematizes the RL-for-LLM paradigm, analyzes computational challenges in training Reasoning Language Models (RLMs), develops a taxonomy of parallelism strategies, and provides practical guidelines for building scalable and cost-effective RLMs.
AI.motivation: RL-for-LLM paradigms like RLVR can significantly improve LLM reasoning capabilities, but training state-of-the-art Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) requires massive computational resources (millions of GPU-hours) and complex multi-model pipelines that stress modern hardware beyond classical supervised training, making RLM training a major parallel/distributed systems challenge.
AI.method: 1) Systematize the RL-for-LLM paradigm and provide compute-centric analysis of prominent post-training frameworks (PPO, GRPO, and variants). 2) Develop a taxonomy of intra- and inter-model parallelism strategies covering traditional techniques and novel forms for multi-model RLM training. 3) Use the work-depth model of parallel computing to make taxonomy rigorous and portable. 4) Analyze existing RLM frameworks to distill practical guidelines.
AI.result: The paper provides a comprehensive systematization of RL-for-LLM training, develops a rigorous taxonomy of parallelism strategies using work-depth model, analyzes computational characteristics of different post-training frameworks, and identifies practical guidelines for scalable RLM development.
AI.conclusion: RLM training is both an algorithmic and distributed systems challenge requiring novel parallelism approaches; the paper provides foundational systematization, computational analysis, and practical guidance for building high-performance, scalable, and cost-effective Reasoning Language Models.

title: Knowing When Not to Reuse: Conditional Experience Transfer in Autonomous LLM Post-Training
summary: Large language models offer broad capabilities, but adapting them to evolving domains, tools, and requirements often entails repeated post-training. Autonomous systems automate parts of this process by proposing updates, training candidates, and using evaluation feedback to select subsequent proposals. As evidence accumulates, a central problem emerges: which past update evidence remains actionable after subsequent training has changed the parent model? An update's effect depends on its parent, data, and training stage. Treating past success as context-free permission can waste compute. If the resulting child is promoted, it can also degrade the subsequent training trajectory. We formulate this problem as conditional experience transfer and introduce Boundary-Calibrated Intervention Transfer (BCIT), a method that authorizes experience reuse before weight-changing training. BCIT binds an observed effect to its source context, checks applicability conditions, vetoes candidates with named hard conflicts, and obtains current-state evidence through a bounded training trial when needed. Fully trained candidates still face a shared adoption rule, and only observed events extend memory. On one 4B model adapted across finance reasoning, text-to-SQL, and function calling, candidate updates exhibit heterogeneous target and retention effects across the evaluated contexts. Under matched candidates, evidence, and compute, BCIT authorizes fewer harmful updates and attains higher equal-budget final-model quality than the evaluated alternatives. These results support treating experience authorization as a distinct problem in autonomous post-training.

AI.tldr: BCIT is a method that improves autonomous post-training of LLMs by intelligently transferring past update experiences to new contexts, preventing harmful updates and improving final model quality.
AI.motivation: Current autonomous systems for adapting LLMs treat past update successes as context-free, which wastes compute resources and can degrade model quality when updates are applied to different parent models or training stages. There's a need for conditional experience transfer that accounts for how update effects depend on their specific context.
AI.method: Boundary-Calibrated Intervention Transfer (BCIT) authorizes experience reuse before weight-changing training by binding observed effects to their source context, checking applicability conditions, vetoing candidates with hard conflicts, and obtaining current-state evidence through bounded training trials when needed.
AI.result: On a 4B model adapted across finance reasoning, text-to-SQL, and function calling domains, BCIT authorized fewer harmful updates and achieved higher final-model quality under equal compute budgets compared to alternatives, demonstrating heterogeneous target and retention effects across contexts.
AI.conclusion: Experience authorization should be treated as a distinct problem in autonomous post-training, and BCIT provides an effective framework for conditional experience transfer that improves update efficiency and model quality.

title: Soft Active Electromyography Interface for Machine Learning-Enabled Silent Speech Recognition
summary: Silent speech recognition (SSR) provides an alternative communication pathway in the absence of audible speech. However, conventional approaches are limited by the need for constant facial attachment, privacy concerns, and unstable signal acquisition. Here, we propose a soft, active electromyography (EMG) interface that enables word-level SSR using machine learning. Worn on the hand, the device uses a fingertip electrode that can be positioned near the lips to acquire EMG signals only when needed. The interface integrates liquid metal (LM) interconnects, transparent flexible printed circuit (FPC) electrodes, and elastomer encapsulation to ensure high mechanical stability during finger motion. A deep neural network trained on these stable signals achieved a mean accuracy of 97.2 $\pm$ 1.3% across three subjects in classifying a 30-word vocabulary, demonstrating robust linguistic discrimination. Furthermore, real-time drone control validates the practicality of this approach in noisy and privacy-sensitive environments where conventional voice recognition fails. This study highlights the potential of soft, wearable EMG systems as secure and intuitive human-machine interfaces.

AI.tldr: A soft wearable EMG interface on the fingertip enables accurate silent speech recognition through machine learning for privacy-sensitive environments.
AI.motivation: Current silent speech recognition systems have limitations: they require constant facial attachment (which is inconvenient), raise privacy concerns, and suffer from unstable signal acquisition. There's a need for more practical, privacy-preserving, and reliable alternatives.
AI.method: Developed a soft, active EMG interface worn on the hand with a fingertip electrode that can be positioned near lips when needed. The device integrates liquid metal interconnects, transparent flexible printed circuit electrodes, and elastomer encapsulation for mechanical stability during finger motion. A deep neural network was trained on these stable EMG signals.
AI.result: The system achieved a mean accuracy of 97.2 ± 1.3% across three subjects in classifying a 30-word vocabulary. Real-time drone control demonstrated practical application in noisy and privacy-sensitive environments where conventional voice recognition fails.
AI.conclusion: This study demonstrates the potential of soft, wearable EMG systems as secure and intuitive human-machine interfaces that overcome limitations of conventional silent speech recognition approaches, offering privacy-preserving communication in sensitive environments.

title: Graph-Guided Selective Unlearning for Language Models: Controlling Support Routes Beyond Forget Seeds
summary: Enterprises fine-tune language models on proprietary data that may later require removal due to privacy, contractual, or compliance obligations. Selective unlearning removes requested knowledge while preserving model utility, offering a practical alternative to full retraining, but existing methods treat the explicitly identified forget examples as the complete deletion scope. This is insufficient when target knowledge remains recoverable through paraphrases, aliases, or neighboring training examples. We propose GRAPHSU, a graph-guided controller that expands the deletion scope beyond forget seeds by constructing a weighted support-route graph, propagating deletion pressure through it, and applying graded forgetting strengths to high-risk neighbors. On the Task of Fictitious Unlearning (TOFU), a synthetic author-profile question-answering benchmark, and PISTOL, a structural-unlearning benchmark built around interconnected factual samples, with GPT-2 Medium and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, GRAPHSU achieves the lowest utility-feasible soft leakage across all deletion settings, reducing leakage by up to 49.5 percentage points over a matched seed-only baseline, demonstrating that effective enterprise unlearning requires controlling support routes, not just forget seeds.

AI.tldr: GRAPHSU is a graph-guided controller for selective unlearning that expands deletion scope beyond explicit forget examples by propagating deletion pressure through weighted support-route graphs, achieving up to 49.5% reduction in leakage compared to seed-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Enterprises need to remove knowledge from fine-tuned language models for privacy, contractual, or compliance reasons, but current selective unlearning methods only delete explicitly identified examples, leaving knowledge recoverable through paraphrases, aliases, or neighboring training examples.
AI.method: GRAPHSU constructs a weighted support-route graph to expand deletion scope beyond forget seeds, propagates deletion pressure through the graph, and applies graded forgetting strengths to high-risk neighbors using graph-guided control.
AI.result: On TOFU (synthetic author-profile QA) and PISTOL (structural-unlearning) benchmarks with GPT-2 Medium and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, GRAPHSU achieves lowest utility-feasible soft leakage across all deletion settings, reducing leakage by up to 49.5 percentage points over seed-only baselines.
AI.conclusion: Effective enterprise unlearning requires controlling support routes (knowledge connections) in addition to forget seeds, as demonstrated by GRAPHSU's significant improvement over traditional seed-only approaches.

title: Unifying Detection and Adaptation in Task-Free Continual Learning
summary: To mitigate catastrophic forgetting in downstream continual learning (CL) for large language models (LLMs), existing methods typically constrain parameter updates or introduce task-specific adaptation modules. However, these methods often rely on explicit task boundaries during training, limiting their applicability to realistic task-free scenarios. In this paper, we propose a \textbf{Fi}sher-guided \textbf{uni}fied (\textbf{FiUni}) framework for batch-level task detection and parameter-efficient continual adaptation. FiUni is motivated by a key observation about the Fisher information matrix (FIM) of pre-trained models: the orthogonality among the principal subspaces of its Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (K-FAC) approximation, estimated from a small number of downstream task samples, can reflect the similarity between different tasks. Based on this observation, FiUni constructs FIM-derived frozen subspaces to guide low-rank adaptation (LoRA), while matching the Fisher principal subspace of each incoming batch window with historical subspaces. This enables FiUni to adaptively determine whether to reuse existing knowledge, expand a related subspace, or create a new subspace, dynamically balancing knowledge sharing and task isolation. Experiments show that FiUni can effectively infer latent batch-level task affiliations and achieve competitive performance against advanced task-aware CL methods with fewer trainable parameters.

AI.tldr: FiUni framework uses Fisher information matrix to detect tasks and adapt LLMs for continual learning without explicit task boundaries, enabling efficient knowledge reuse and isolation.
AI.motivation: Existing continual learning methods for LLMs rely on explicit task boundaries during training, which limits their applicability to realistic task-free scenarios where tasks arrive without clear separation.
AI.method: FiUni uses Fisher information matrix (specifically K-FAC approximation) to analyze task similarity by examining orthogonality of principal subspaces. It constructs FIM-derived frozen subspaces to guide LoRA adaptation, while matching Fisher principal subspaces of incoming batch windows with historical ones to determine whether to reuse, expand, or create new subspaces.
AI.result: FiUni effectively infers latent batch-level task affiliations and achieves competitive performance against advanced task-aware continual learning methods while using fewer trainable parameters.
AI.conclusion: The FiUni framework provides an effective solution for task-free continual learning in LLMs by using Fisher information for task detection and subspace management, dynamically balancing knowledge sharing and task isolation without requiring explicit task boundaries.

title: AgentFold: Closed-Loop Agentic Search for Protein Folding Model Design
summary: Scientific LLM agents have shown promise in literature reasoning, tool use, and experiment planning, but it remains unclear whether they can autonomously improve large, tightly coupled scientific machine-learning systems through executable code changes and computationally expensive validation. We study this question in protein folding, where progress requires coordinated architectural modifications, multi-objective evaluation, and domain-aware interpretation. We present AgentFold, a multi-agent framework that formulates folding-model development as a closed-loop search over executable code variants. Starting from ESMFold, AgentFold proposes hypotheses, implements and debugs code-level modifications, evaluates model variants, analyzes experimental outcomes, and stores both successful and failed interventions in structured memory. An MCTS-style policy allocates computational resources across high-scoring search branches. On an engineering-scale protein-folding codebase comprising more than 2,000 lines of code, AgentFold explores approximately 80 model variants using approximately 5,000 GPU-hours and 170 million LLM tokens. Under a matched computational budget, AgentFold improves the best lDDT by 7.5% over independent Codex proposals and outperforms a random-search control. Beyond model improvement, the resulting intervention traces reveal recurring empirical design patterns: stable gains tend to arise from early, soft, learnable priors and gated refinement, whereas direct geometric perturbations and geometry-conditioned feedback often destabilize training. The code and experimental resources are publicly available at https://github.com/lmqfly/AgentFold.

AI.tldr: AgentFold is a multi-agent framework that autonomously improves protein folding models by searching through executable code modifications, outperforming baseline approaches while revealing design patterns for stable model improvements.
AI.motivation: While scientific LLM agents have shown promise in various scientific tasks, it remains unclear whether they can autonomously improve large, tightly coupled scientific machine-learning systems through executable code changes and computationally expensive validation. The authors investigate this in protein folding, which requires coordinated architectural modifications, multi-objective evaluation, and domain-aware interpretation.
AI.method: AgentFold is a multi-agent framework that formulates folding-model development as a closed-loop search over executable code variants. Starting from ESMFold, it proposes hypotheses, implements and debugs code-level modifications, evaluates model variants, analyzes experimental outcomes, and stores both successful and failed interventions in structured memory. An MCTS-style policy allocates computational resources across high-scoring search branches.
AI.result: On an engineering-scale protein-folding codebase (2,000+ lines of code), AgentFold explores ~80 model variants using ~5,000 GPU-hours and 170 million LLM tokens. It improves the best lDDT by 7.5% over independent Codex proposals and outperforms a random-search control under matched computational budget. The intervention traces reveal design patterns: stable gains arise from early, soft, learnable priors and gated refinement, while direct geometric perturbations and geometry-conditioned feedback often destabilize training.
AI.conclusion: AgentFold demonstrates that LLM agents can autonomously improve large-scale scientific ML systems through coordinated code modifications. The framework not only achieves measurable improvements in protein folding but also generates valuable insights about architectural design patterns that lead to stable model enhancements.

title: Emotional Preferences as Goal-Priority Regulation
summary: A core question in decision-making for agents is whether the relative priorities of competing lower-level objectives can be determined by emotional preferences autonomously generated by higher-level goals, rather than being externally prespecified. Under changing external environments and evolving internal states, emotions play an important functional role in regulating the relative priorities of competing goals. Inspired by the goal-directed theory of emotion, this paper studies how such preference regulation can be computationally realized through reinforcement learning. We first propose a conception of emergent emotional preference: a high-level goal autonomously induces state-dependent preferences over competing lower-level objectives. This conception is built upon a framework consisting of a multi-objective reinforcement learning inner controller and an outer preference generator. The inner controller provides a repertoire of preference-conditioned goal-directed behaviors, while the outer preference generator learns a mapping from the current state to objective preferences through reinforcement learning on a high-level goal. We operationalize emotional preference as a state-dependent regulation of relative goal priorities that emerges through optimization. Furthermore, we characterize the policy space induced by preference regulation and derive an upper bound on the optimality gap in terms of the representation error of the inner behavioral repertoire. We show that the gap vanishes when the optimal policy can be represented by the available preference-conditioned policies. Experiments in self-constructed multi-objective exploration environments show that the learned preference function exhibits contextual priority switching, graded trade-offs, and temporal persistence, and outperforms the evaluated fixed-preference and handcrafted-preference strategies.

AI.tldr: Emotional preferences can autonomously regulate competing goal priorities through multi-objective RL, outperforming fixed and handcrafted preference strategies.
AI.motivation: In dynamic environments, agents need to autonomously regulate relative priorities of competing lower-level objectives based on emotional preferences generated from higher-level goals, rather than relying on externally prespecified priorities.
AI.method: Two-level framework: inner multi-objective RL controller provides preference-conditioned goal-directed behaviors; outer preference generator learns state-dependent preference mapping through RL on high-level goals. Emotional preference emerges as state-dependent regulation of goal priorities.
AI.result: Characterized policy space from preference regulation, derived optimality gap bound based on inner behavioral repertoire representation error. Experiments show learned preferences exhibit contextual priority switching, graded trade-offs, temporal persistence, and outperform fixed and handcrafted preference strategies.
AI.conclusion: Emotional preferences can be computationally realized through multi-objective RL to autonomously regulate competing goal priorities, enabling adaptive behavior in changing environments based on higher-level goals.

title: Discovering Relationships in Data Lakes Using Large Language Models: An Industrial Case
summary: Data lakes rely on metadata to remain usable, yet this meta data is often limited or weakly informative for column relationship discovery, especially in ERP-derived datasets with coded or abbreviated schema labels. We propose ColRel, a two-stage method that builds column embeddings from metadata and data available at ingestion time. In difficult cases, such as coded schemata, business dictionaries help better interpret column names and support the generation of short natural-language descriptions used in the second stage. Experiments on public benchmarks and an industrial ERP dataset show that ColRel is particularly effective in semantically related, weak-signal settings.

AI.tldr: ColRel: A two-stage method for discovering column relationships in data lakes using embeddings from metadata and data, with business dictionary support for coded schemata.
AI.motivation: Data lakes often have limited or weakly informative metadata for column relationship discovery, especially in ERP-derived datasets with coded or abbreviated schema labels that make relationship discovery challenging.
AI.method: A two-stage method that builds column embeddings from both metadata and data available at ingestion time. For coded schemata, it uses business dictionaries to interpret column names and generate short natural-language descriptions for the second stage.
AI.result: Experiments on public benchmarks and an industrial ERP dataset demonstrate that ColRel is particularly effective in semantically related, weak-signal settings where traditional methods struggle.
AI.conclusion: ColRel provides an effective solution for column relationship discovery in data lakes with limited metadata, especially for complex ERP datasets with coded schema labels, outperforming existing approaches in challenging weak-signal scenarios.

title: Tabular Deep Learning for Algorithmic Trading: Cross-Regime Bayesian Optimisation for Equity Signal Generation
summary: Algorithmic trading now represents a market exceeding $20 billion, where even marginal gains in signal robustness can translate into economically significant returns. Existing evaluations of equity prediction models do not explicitly target regime robustness during hyperparameter selection. Five model classes are trained on daily observations from approximately 300 large-cap US equities over eleven years, with Bayesian optimisation configured to target trading performance across three statistically different market regimes. Regime-robust hyperparameter selection is associated with out-of-sample generalisation, as signal precision remains above the random baseline across all four quarters of the test period, and portfolio performance slowly degrades under simulated input noise before collapsing beyond a defined threshold. No individual tabular deep learning architecture outperforms gradient-boosted trees, but combining XGBoost and TabNet using rank aggregation produces a Hybrid ensemble with an annualised return of 51.26%, a Sharpe ratio of 2.44, and a statistically significant CAPM alpha of 0.423 (p = 0.011). A near-zero beta indicates this outperformance is driven by stock selection, not market exposure. Alternative data plays a secondary role once technical and fundamental features are accounted for, as well as contributing more strongly on the short side than the long, and varies by model class. An interactive application makes these results explorable in real time, with live data integration the remaining step toward practical deployment.

AI.tldr: Hybrid ensemble combining XGBoost and TabNet with regime-robust hyperparameter optimization achieves superior algorithmic trading performance with 51.26% annual returns and statistically significant alpha.
AI.motivation: Algorithmic trading is a $20+ billion market where small improvements in signal robustness can yield significant economic returns. Existing equity prediction models don't explicitly target regime robustness during hyperparameter selection.
AI.method: Trained five model classes on daily observations from ~300 large-cap US equities over 11 years. Used Bayesian optimization configured to target trading performance across three statistically different market regimes. Combined XGBoost and TabNet using rank aggregation to create a Hybrid ensemble.
AI.result: Hybrid ensemble achieved 51.26% annualized return, Sharpe ratio of 2.44, and statistically significant CAPM alpha of 0.423 (p=0.011). Near-zero beta indicates outperformance from stock selection rather than market exposure. Alternative data played secondary role after accounting for technical/fundamental features. Regime-robust hyperparameter selection showed strong out-of-sample generalization.
AI.conclusion: Regime-robust hyperparameter optimization is crucial for sustainable trading strategies. Combining gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost) with tabular deep learning (TabNet) via ensemble methods yields superior performance. Alternative data provides complementary signals but is secondary to traditional features. The approach demonstrates practical potential with interactive application developed for real-time exploration.

title: DEEPCHART: How Far are LLMs from Faithful Data-Science Chart Generation?
summary: Faithful chart generation in real-world data-science workflows requires grounding visualizations in scattered evidence, computing chart-ready quantities, and rendering them accurately. Modern LLMs can produce visually plausible, instruction-compliant charts, yet data-level hallucinations remain difficult to detect in long, noisy, and multimodal contexts. To measure this gap, we introduce DEEPCHART, an expert-annotated benchmark of 1,482 task-conditioned chart-generation instances drawn from real-world scientific papers, financial filings, and ecosystem reports. DEEPCHART formulates chart generation as an Extract--Reason--Visualize pipeline and evaluates source-data extraction, derived-data reasoning, and chart rendering stage by stage. Experiments with state-of-the-art models show that visually plausible charts often conceal data-level hallucinations, with extraction and reasoning errors common in realistic long and multimodal settings. These findings suggest that larger context windows alone are insufficient; faithful chart generation also requires reliable evidence extraction and quantitative reasoning before rendering. Our benchmark and associated resources are available at https://github.com/tangdouer1005/DeepChart.

AI.tldr: DEEPCHART is a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based chart generation, revealing that visually plausible charts often contain hidden data-level hallucinations that current models struggle with despite larger context windows.
AI.motivation: Real-world chart generation requires grounding visualizations in scattered evidence and accurate data computation, but modern LLMs produce visually plausible charts while still making data-level hallucinations that are difficult to detect in complex, multimodal contexts.
AI.method: The authors created DEEPCHART, an expert-annotated benchmark of 1,482 task-conditioned chart-generation instances from real-world sources (scientific papers, financial filings, ecosystem reports). They formulated chart generation as an Extract–Reason–Visualize pipeline and evaluated models across source-data extraction, derived-data reasoning, and chart rendering stages.
AI.result: Experiments with state-of-the-art models show that visually plausible charts often conceal data-level hallucinations. Extraction and reasoning errors are common in realistic long and multimodal settings, indicating that larger context windows alone are insufficient for faithful chart generation.
AI.conclusion: Faithful chart generation requires reliable evidence extraction and quantitative reasoning before rendering, not just larger context windows. The benchmark and resources are publicly available for advancing research in this area.

title: Cone Extended Rayleigh Quotients for Directed Graph Learning: Minimax Spectral Certificates, Sensitivity, and Adaptive Control
summary:
Directed graph learning naturally leads to trainable nonsymmetric propagation operators with distinct right and left spectral structures. Building on the two-sided cone Rayleigh framework for generalized pencils \[ B_θ-λG, \] we develop a learning-oriented methodology for spectral certification, sensitivity analysis, and control without requiring symmetry, nonnegativity, or cone preservation. In the positive-orthant setting, computable lower and upper cone bounds provide an a posteriori enclosure of a distinguished cone level, while smooth soft-min/max surrogates preserve rigorous one-sided bounds with explicit approximation errors and remain differentiable with respect to the trainable parameters.
  For a simple interior level, the right and left modes satisfy \[ Dλ_C(B)[H]=v_C^T H u_C, \] yielding first-order optimal graph-supported interventions under prescribed perturbation budgets and motivating adaptive spectral control. Numerical experiments demonstrate the applicability of the approach beyond cone-preserving operators and in directed learning settings. Signed nonsymmetric perturbations reveal a transition from interior eigenpairs to boundary complementary quasi-pairs, including non-spectral cone levels, while controlled experiments show that symmetrization can remove predictive information carried solely by edge direction.
  On the directed Cora citation network, adaptive recomputation of the right--left sensitivity reduces the distinguished spectral level by approximately $21.5\%$ under a cumulative edge-weight reduction budget of $0.5\%$, with no observed change in test accuracy for the trained model and data split considered.

AI.tldr: A learning-oriented spectral certification and control framework for directed graph neural networks, enabling adaptive intervention without requiring symmetry or nonnegativity, with demonstrated effectiveness on citation networks.
AI.motivation: Directed graph learning involves nonsymmetric operators with distinct left/right spectral structures, but existing methods lack rigorous spectral certification and control for these asymmetric systems without imposing restrictive assumptions like symmetry or nonnegativity.
AI.method: Develops a two-sided cone Rayleigh framework for generalized pencils, using computable cone bounds for a posteriori enclosures of distinguished spectral levels, smooth soft-min/max surrogates with explicit error bounds, and first-order sensitivity analysis for optimal graph interventions under perturbation budgets.
AI.result: The approach works beyond cone-preserving operators, reveals transitions from interior eigenpairs to boundary quasi-pairs, shows symmetrization can remove directional predictive information, and on Cora citation network achieves 21.5% spectral reduction with only 0.5% edge-weight reduction without affecting test accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The learning-oriented methodology provides effective spectral certification and control for directed graph neural networks, enabling adaptive interventions that preserve directional information while optimizing spectral properties, with promising applications in graph learning beyond symmetric settings.

title: Categorizer Automata for Discounted-Sum Payoffs
summary: Categorizing continuous data into discrete bins is a fundamental operation in artificial intelligence. We introduce the categorizer automaton, a deterministic automaton that reads an infinite sequence of rewards and identifies which of finitely many bins contains its discounted sum. Categorizer automata generalize comparator automata, the special case of two bins, which have already proven useful in quantitative synthesis. Our main technical contribution is the construction of a categorizer automaton whose state space is linear in the number of bins, rather than exponential as obtained by a cross-product of comparator automata. We then apply categorizer automata to Markov decision processes, where they allow one to synthesize policies that maximize the expected utility of a discounted-sum payoff for utility functions that may be discontinuous. For piecewise-constant utility functions, the resulting algorithm is exact and runs in pseudo-polynomial time. For piecewise-Lipschitz utility functions, a class that includes any utility with bounded slope between finitely many jumps, it again runs in pseudo-polynomial time and yields an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy. We also show that the synthesis problem considered is PSPACE-hard already for piecewise-constant utilities.

AI.tldr: A new categorizer automaton that bins continuous discounted-sum rewards into discrete categories, enabling efficient synthesis of policies for MDPs with discontinuous utility functions.
AI.motivation: Categorizing continuous data into discrete bins is fundamental in AI. Existing comparator automata only handle two bins (binary classification), limiting their applicability to problems requiring multiple discrete categories for utility functions in quantitative synthesis.
AI.method: Introduce categorizer automata - deterministic automata that read infinite reward sequences and classify their discounted sums into finitely many bins. Construct a categorizer automaton with linear state space (vs exponential cross-product construction). Apply to Markov decision processes for policy synthesis with discontinuous utility functions.
AI.result: For piecewise-constant utility functions: exact algorithm in pseudo-polynomial time. For piecewise-Lipschitz utility functions: ε-optimal policy in pseudo-polynomial time. The synthesis problem is PSPACE-hard for piecewise-constant utilities.
AI.conclusion: Categorizer automata provide an efficient framework for handling multi-category classification of discounted-sum rewards, enabling practical synthesis of policies for MDPs with discontinuous utility functions while establishing computational complexity bounds.

title: TRACE-CRC: Trajectory-Adaptive Conformal Risk Control for Multi-Step Channel State Information Prediction
comment: Published in Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (PMLR), volume 329, Conformal and Probabilistic Prediction with Applications (COPA 2026)
summary: Reliable prediction of time-varying channel state information (CSI) is essential for efficient wireless communication. Each CSI frame is a matrix-valued representation of the wireless channel response, and a sequence of CSI frames forms a temporal channel trajectory. Modern deep learning-based CSI predictors, however, often provide only point predictions and lack calibrated uncertainty estimates. This limitation is particularly problematic in multi-step CSI prediction, where the target is a sequence of future CSI matrices, and downstream decisions such as beamforming or scheduling may fail if any part of the predicted trajectory is unreliable. We propose trajectory-adaptive calibration and error profiling with conformal risk control (TRACE-CRC), a method for trajectory-aware uncertainty quantification in multi-step CSI prediction. TRACE-CRC constructs Frobenius-norm uncertainty balls around predicted CSI matrices and controls the risk that at least one future frame is uncovered. Instead of calibrating each future step independently, TRACE-CRC combines future-step-dependent error profiling, trajectory difficulty stratification, and learn-then-test (LTT) risk control. Empirically, TRACE-CRC achieves reliable trajectory-level coverage with substantially smaller uncertainty balls than conservative multi-step corrections, while avoiding the trajectory undercoverage of compact stepwise and adaptive conformal baselines.

AI.tldr: TRACE-CRC is a method for trajectory-aware uncertainty quantification in multi-step CSI prediction that constructs uncertainty balls around predicted channel matrices and controls the risk of missing any future frame.
AI.motivation: Current deep learning-based CSI predictors provide only point predictions without calibrated uncertainty estimates, which is problematic for multi-step prediction where downstream decisions (beamforming, scheduling) may fail if any part of the predicted trajectory is unreliable.
AI.method: TRACE-CRC combines future-step-dependent error profiling, trajectory difficulty stratification, and learn-then-test (LTT) risk control to construct Frobenius-norm uncertainty balls around predicted CSI matrices while controlling the risk that at least one future frame is uncovered.
AI.result: Empirically, TRACE-CRC achieves reliable trajectory-level coverage with substantially smaller uncertainty balls than conservative multi-step corrections, while avoiding the trajectory undercoverage of compact stepwise and adaptive conformal baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed trajectory-adaptive calibration with conformal risk control provides effective uncertainty quantification for multi-step CSI prediction, addressing the limitations of existing methods that either lack trajectory awareness or use overly conservative approaches.

title: AI Control Scientist: LLM-driven Agentic System for Automated Control Design
summary: Control system design is critical for modern industry, such as chemical process temperature regulation and aero-engine control. However,traditional control design workflows rely heavily on expert knowledge and extensive manual parameter tuning, resulting in limited efficiency and scalability. To this end, this paper proposes AI Control Scientist (AICS), the first large language model (LLM)-driven agent capable of automatically generating optimized controller from language design requirements. Specifically, a Task Modeling Agent interprets user requirements to engineering constraints; a Controller Design Agent generate candidate controller structures and executable code; and a Parameter Tuning Agent refine controller parameters under closed-loop performance criteria. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed agentic system can automatically generate multiple representative control systems, outperforms existing automated baselines in both design success rate and optimization efficiency. This work has the potential to transform control system design from human-driven to agent-driven, paving the way for model predictive control and other advanced control systems design.

AI.tldr: AICS is an LLM-driven agent system that automatically generates optimized controllers from language requirements, outperforming existing automated methods and potentially transforming control system design workflows.
AI.motivation: Traditional control system design workflows rely heavily on expert knowledge and extensive manual parameter tuning, which limits efficiency and scalability. There's a need to automate this process to overcome these limitations.
